speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: VISIT TO OTTAWA BY SIR WINSTON CHURCHILL AND MR. EDEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I should inform the house about the exchange of messages with London concerning the visit by Sir Winston Churchill and Mr. Eden to Washington at the end of next week. As soon as we heard that a date had been set for that visit we made inquiries through the office of the United Kingdom High Commissioner here in Ottawa and through our own High Commissioner in the office of commonwealth relations in London as to the possibility of their coming to Ottawa on the occasion of their visit to this continent.
Yesterday morning I received personally from Sir Winston Churchill a very cordial message in which he said he always enjoyed a conference in Canada but could not make any plans at the present time. Following that message I had this message sent to the Secretary of State for Commonwealth Relations of the British government:
Having heard that Sir Winston and Mr. Eden are coming to Washington, my colleagues and I would like to assure them that, if it were convenient for them to visit Ottawa on their way back, they would be most warmly welcomed and that we would much appreciate the opportunity of hearing direct from them their appreciation of the present situation.
I quite understand, however, Sir Winston's difficulty about making plans at present for such a visit and I would not like him to feel any embarrassment if circumstances made it necessary for him to decline our invitation at this time.
This morning I received this personal message from Sir Winston which I am glad to communicate to the house:
So glad to get your telegram. I have every hope of coming to Ottawa for a day or a day and a half during the 29th of June, 30th of June and 1st of July, if it is convenient to you. Mr. Eden, to whom I have spoken, will be delighted to come too. I do not want any public meeting but we shall be honoured to meet your cabinet.

subtopic: VISIT TO OTTAWA BY SIR WINSTON CHURCHILL AND MR. EDEN
speechtext:
May I ask the Prime Minister whether it would be feasible to have any sort of commonwealth conference at that time in view of the fact that Sir Winston
Churchill will just have completed very important discussions with the President of the United States?

subtopic: VISIT TO OTTAWA BY SIR WINSTON CHURCHILL AND MR. EDEN
speechtext: I do not think so, Mr. Speaker. I think this means that we will have an opportunity of hearing from Sir Winston and Mr. Eden their appreciation of the situation as they see it at this time. There would be no opportunity for bringing representatives of other commonwealth countries here, and that would not conform with the tone of this exchange of messages. I understand the visit Sir Winston and Mr. Eden are making to Mr. Eisenhower is an informal personal week-end visit, and that Sir Winston and Mr. Eden hope that it may be possible for them, on their way back, to spend a day or a day and a half here having the same kind of informal discussions with us about the present situation.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext: I should like to have the minister say something about the dominion bureau of statistics. I have received great help from it myself and appreciate its value very highly. There is one thing, however, which has been mentioned in the house before.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext:
Order. May I ask hon.
members to please maintain silence. It is impossible to hear the hon. member who has the floor.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext:
I am speaking loud
enough. The trouble is that other people are speaking too loud. I want to raise the question of the extraordinary discrepancy which exists between the figures put out by the dominion bureau of statistics, being a part of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and the Department of Labour in the matter of employment and unemployment. It seems to me to be obvious that unemployment is one of the most important matters which face us at the moment, and it seems an extraordinary thing to me that we have this terrific discrepancy in figures. It has been explained in a way but not in a way with which anyone in my opinion should be satisfied.
One department uses the phrase "persons without jobs and seeking work", and the other uses a different phrase which I forget for the moment. We get figures not varying by 10 per cent or 20 per cent but sometimes by 50 per cent or more. It may be satisfactory to the departments concerned. They may have their ways of making their own mental reservations and explanations, but surely it is entirely unsatisfactory from the point of view of the public. Certainly it is entirely unsatisfactory from the point of view of labour because it means that they never have firm ground on which to discuss the matter. It is one thing to discuss the question of unemployment with the government if unemployment is 10 per cent. It is an entirely different thing if it is 5 per cent.
Further, I have been reading in the Labour Gazette for April a very interesting article about seasonal unemployment. There is a long discussion there and some suggestions are laid down as to how seasonal unemployment shall be assessed. Of course seasonal unemployment is the reason that has been given for the situation, but we are now in June and I do not think that the defence of seasonal unemployment can be of any further value. I would ask the minister to give us a full explanation of why the difference does exist. I am not blaming the dominion bureau of statistics at all. I assume it is done under instructions because they have got to be given a policy in order to work out a figure. I assume they are under instructions as they quite properly should be. I understand for example that they do not include figures of people temporarily out of work; people who have been let out but with instructions that they are to come back at the end of thirty days.
But these people are certainly out of work at the moment, and I take it also that even if all of them go back at the end of thirty

days it is not reasonable to assume that the same thing has not happened to a lot of others in the interval. In other words, the thing rolls around. I understand that the Department of Labour does include those figures, and if they do I take it that is on the assumption that if you have tens of thousands of people temporarily out of work in May you are not going to find a situation in June where all those tens of thousands of people have come back and where no others are in the position that the first lot were in during the preceding month.
In other words, so far as my judgment goes, I find the figures of the Department of Labour very much more realistic than those of the Department of Trade and Commerce. I think we should try to get to the bottom of it because it is a very important matter. The minister accused me the other day of being a pessimist. I hope I am not. Pessimists are a nuisance to everybody, and I do not want to regard myself as being in that category. I want to be a little optimist, but on the other hand I cannot go around like some members of the house and, when I am asked the reason for my faith, just say: "Well, C. D. said so". There are a lot of people in the house who think that when they have said that, the matter is settled. To me that is a very important piece of evidence, but I do not regard it as absolutely the last and final word, not necessarily.
Therefore I hope the minister will have regard for my weakness, for my quality of optimism which is not so great as his and which wants to be optimism plus reason. I should like an attempt to be made, which I have not heard done before, to reconcile these two figures and to make sense of them because, as somebody said, at the moment there seems to be a kind of cold war between these two departments.
Mr. Hov/e (Pori Arthur): I presume my hon. friend prefers the Department of Labour figures because they suit him better as a basis for argument, but he is really making an analysis of two different things. The Department of Labour figures show the number of people looking for jobs on a particular day. There would be no harm, and it would be quite in order for my hon. friend to go to the nearest labour office and put his name down as one seeking a job. He might find a better one than he has.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext:
Not after all we members have said about being fully employed.
Supply-Trade and Commerce

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext: Probably the bureau of statistics would put him down as employed, even though he might be seeking a job. There, you have the situation.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext: He is a sort of temporary permanent.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext:
Yes, quite right. We have a situation where people register for jobs while they are employed. We also have a situation where a man will retire from the railroad on a pension and then put himself down as seeking a job. Would you list him as unemployed? The bureau of statistics would refer to him as a man outside the labour force. He had retired. Nevertheless, the labour department would include his name as an applicant for a job.
I do not believe there is any harm in telling the house as a matter of interest that by arrangement with the labour department we had a survey made of a list of those applying for jobs as registered in the labour department. We did not inform the field men that there was anything particular about the list we sent down to them, but they thought the results were sufficiently odd to warrant a special report to the Ottawa headquarters. The report said that they found the list most extraordinary; actually over 50 per cent of the people on it were out of work, and they thought the department should know!
The labour survey is made on a scientific basis, and it follows the approved sampling methods of the bureau of statistics. Over 30,000 families are called upon each month, and it is a different 30,000 each time. A report is based on the findings of that survey. If the man is unemployed and seeking work on the day the survey is made, then he is registered as unemployed. A list is made up by expanding that sample survey to cover the working force of Canada. I may say that the bureau of statistics survey is much more complete than the surveys upon which unemployment figures are based in the United States. This survey of 30,000 out of a v/orking force of 5 million is a very much larger sample than is used In the survey of unemployment in the country to the south. We believe the results are correct, so far as it can be determined by sampling methods.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext:
The minister has just explained that in sampling for the purpose of labour statistics different people are interviewed each time. I should like to make some representations to the department on behalf of a group of people who have found that they

Supply-Trade and Commerce suffer considerable inconvenience because of being on the list for sampling, and not being able to get off the list. I am not talking about labour statistics; I am talking about statistics that are sought from various industries through surveys by the bureau of statistics. I realize that when you seek to produce statistics by the sampling method you must select certain people out of each industry for which the survey is conducted who can supply you with the material.
The part to which I object is the fact that some small industries or comparatively small restaurants, with one or two persons in the office, are periodically required to make returns to the bureau of statistics. Despite the fact that they protest that their office staff is not adequate to keep this up indefinitely, they simply cannot get off the list. In some cases, it goes on for a long time. It does not seem right to me that a few people should be saddled with this job of providing statistics for the bureau, while a great many people in the country go scot-free. If you have a small office staff, it is an expensive procedure. It sometimes means you have to hire extra help in order to supply these figures. I am sure many of these people realize the importance of supplying the figures, but they do believe they are being discriminated against.
If they were put on the list for a year and then removed, there would not be too much complaint. However, when they are put on the list indefinitely and they realize they are being forced to supply information to the bureau that their competitor is not forced to supply, they believe there is just cause for complaint. I ask the minister, therefore, to inquire into this matter to see that some people are not forced to continuously supply information.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext:
I would say at once that any information that is gathered by the bureau is entirely confidential. Not long ago we had a case which may interest the house. We were asked by another government for information that the bureau of statistics had. We consulted the bureau, and they said we could not disclose it even privately to another government. It was gathered as private information and could not be released to anyone for any purpose, so the information was not given. There is nothing guarded more carefully in government circles than information gathered by the bureau of statistics.
Every effort has been made to cause the least possible inconvenience in obtaining the statistics that are considered necessary in carrying out the functions of the bureau. We


have now on the questionnaire list business firms of less than $50,000 capitalization. The form for such companies has been simplified so that only one question is asked, and that is quite a simple one. In the case of labour statistics, if anyone objects to answering the questions we simply drop their name from the list and pick another name. I am told that the bureau receives remarkable cooperation from the public in gathering information, and finds very little resentment about giving the information that is required.
I must say I have received no complaints that I recall about any demand from the bureau for information. I am sure our chief statistician will keep in mind the suggestions of the hon. member for Hamilton West to make certain that sampling lists do not include the same name too long. I am told that is not the practice. The practice is, where sampling is performed, to change the lists frequently. I am sure the dominion statistician will look into the complaint and make sure the inconvenience is minimized to the greatest possible extent.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext: The minister must have misunderstood me with reference to the first part of his remarks. I was not talking about the confidential nature of the reports at all. I was making, more or less, a representation on behalf of these small companies. I know, and the minister knows, that if you have a sizeable staff it is easy to juggle jobs around so that someone can compile these statistics. It is, however, a real hardship on the little fellow. Despite the minister's assurance, I know of a few cases where names have been on the list for a long time, and despite their protests. I take it that what is required is that they make a written protest, and their names will be removed, but that has not been the experience of some of these people.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext: The head of the bureau of statistics tells me that he would like very much to have the names of those people, for his confidential guidance. Perhaps my hon. friend would pass those names along.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext: I shall do so.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext:
May I join with the hon. member for Greenwood in paying tribute to the excellent job done by the dominion bureau of statistics. I have seldom if ever known an instance where the bureau was unable to supply information I have tried to get from them. In fact often when one seeks certain information he gets more than he asks for. In short, they do an awfully good job.
In this connection I was a bit surprised the other day to find that certain questions

I had placed on the order paper were answered by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Defence Production, apparently on behalf of the dominion bureau of statistics. They were questions relating to records concerning charges and offences under the Criminal Code. Supply-Trade and Commerce department for not having better roads to assist labourers who travel perhaps 50 miles to and from their work. With all due respect for presidents, in this instance I begin to think that this particular president should be shown a few things.
My point is that in the smaller towns the workers have to travel only short distances, at the outside taking up perhaps only 15 minutes of their time. Walking to work they meet each other-"Hello Bill; hello Jack"- and it is not just a rat race such as we see in the larger cities. Mr. Chairman, in view of what was said a short time ago by the hon. member for Greenwood may I take this opportunity to say just a word about the points he brought up, particularly considering the very fair way in which he dealt with the matter.
Prior to a year ago last fall in the Department of Labour we had been publishing every month figures showing the total number of those seeking employment across Canada. At and prior to that time we in the Department of Labour, as well as my colleagues in other departments, felt that although a true total of workers so listed was coming out of the adding machines in our U.I.C. offices it did not give a clear picture either in winter or in summer.
Consequently we had a very careful study undertaken. Part of that study included a cross-check in different parts of Canada referred to today by my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce. A check of listed unemployed was made to find out if they were actually unemployed. I must say when the results of that check came to my attention it was a surprise as well as a bit of of a shock to me.
Yet, Mr. Chairman, what was found is not surprising when we realize that in our 230 offices, particularly in the winter months when our staffs are busily engaged in interviewing applicants for work and looking after all those complex matters entering into the insurance plan, there is not the time for the staff to con over the lists of applicants to find out by telephone, by letter or by wire which ones may have got work somewhere else, which ones may be listed at other places, and all those pieces of information which would be necessary to strip the lists down to applicants still wanting jobs.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
As a result of that, beginning a year ago December, I believe it was, it was decided that the quarterly announcement made by the dominion bureau of statistics should be enlarged and, if you like, sharpened up, and made into a monthly report based upon the survey the minister outlined a little while ago.
The suggestion was made that the results of that survey, with the new total, might be the only monthly total issued. My personal view was that it would be wrong to do so- and I still feel that way-because ever since 1941 the monthly list showing the total of persons seeking employment has gone out to the public. We have had that for every month. We have not had any other yardstick for every month, except the information we have had only since a year ago last December when the list was begun by the dominion bureau of statistics.
So it was decided in the middle of the winter a year ago last January to issue this as a joint release, providing for the public all the information we had on the subject, including the total number of persons seeking employment as of a given date. The one which will come out within a week will be as of approximately May 20, just as the one which came out around May 20 showed the total as of about April 20. In other words, the figures are about a month old.
Now, there is another factor affecting the total number who are seeking employment. Particularly in the winter months we have found in the cities and towns a keen interest on the part of everyone as to how the picture was going with regard to that city, town or province. By the very nature of it, the dominion bureau of statistics' plan is a nationwide one, and so are the conclusions drawn from that. In the city of Toronto, for instance, the only indicator on the employment situation there today, as compared with three years ago this date, would be that very general one coming from the Department of Labour. I want to take advantage of being on my feet at this time to scotch completely a suggestion that has been made in some quarters that this combined release was over the dead body of the Department of Labour or the Minister of Labour. It was nothing of the sort. As a matter of fact it was we who suggested that the study take place and we have co-operated and will co-operate in every way to provide the best information we can. On the one hand, a careful survey is made by D.B.S., an agency of government that has had great experience and in which all the members have complete confidence; and, on the other, a simple total through U.I.C. of those who are applying at any given time.
I should like to tell the committee that if it is possible to narrow the gap or give more


precise information, we will certainly do it. I can tell the committee that I have gone over the comparable reports which are issued south of the line from month to month, and I must say that the three or four that are produced there do not add any more precise information than we are giving. I am sure it will be realized by the hon. member for Greenwood that it would be impossible, even if you carried out a complete census in Canada, to say exactly how many men and women are unemployed on this 17th day of June. By the time the callers went around to the doors and found out, the figures for people behind them on whom they had called would be out of date before totals could be got. We have got to give the best information that can be made available.

speechtext: I should like to ask a question on this item. To what extent does the bureau of statistics gather information in the rural areas of a province like Saskatchewan? The reason I ask the question is that in my area there was a man going around visiting ever so many farms. He called on the fourth or fifth one in the areas surrounding the villages, and he also made a canvass of the villagers in that area. He took one out of so many houses as he went down the street. To what extent is that being done throughout Saskatchewan? Those statistics were gathered from a good many people who would probably list themselves as unemployed on the farms because they were under the impression that if they listed themselves as unemployed they would get a job in town in the winter or in the logging camps, or something of that nature. That would affect the unemployment picture. They are not unemployed now of course. My reason for asking the question is to find out how that might influence the unemployment picture. Does the bureau of statistics have quite a group of men doing that type of work in Saskatchewan? The man I have in mind lives on a farm. From time to time he jumps in his car and goes around and gathers this information.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES

I am told that we do make a survey of rural Saskatchewan. If he were away from home and working as a logger and were out of work as a logger, he would be registered as unemployed. In that class of labour, that shifts between the farm and the forest industry, there is bound to be a discrepancy in labour figures. In my own district many loggers live on little farms and

their business is logging. Nevertheless, if they are not logging at the time of the survey, they would be registered as unemployed in that area.

Mr. Chairman, there are a few brief remarks I would like to make on this item. During the recent discussion in this house on Bill No. 7 dealing with the Criminal Code the question of death on the highways was discussed from time to time and some intimation was given that perhaps next session a further discussion of the matter of traffic fatalities and problems relating thereto would be undertaken. I believe the minister even intimated that there might possibly be some sort of conference with the attorneys general of the various provinces in view of the jurisdictional problems which arise relative to this question.
In view of the fact that the question of accidents and death on the highways has become increasingly grave in this country, I am wondering whether the minister might consider recommending to the dominion bureau of statistics that they compile more complete figures with respect to motor vehicle accidents and traffic offences throughout the country.
The figures we have at present in the Canada Year Book are meagre when one considers the magnitude of the problem involved, and though I realize it may be a difficult and expensive job in obtaining this information I think in view of the fact that this is such a major problem it might be well worth while.
For example, there is no break-down of the type of traffic offences. The Canada Year Book at page 304 gives by province the number of convictions against breaches of the traffic regulations, but it does not give any break-down of the variety of accidents, whether they are due to careless driving, speeding, failing to stop at a stop sign, or merely neglecting to have a licence renewed.
I think there might be other interesting break-downs such as the age groups of the persons involved in traffic accidents; and another and very important break-down would be one showing how many involve

Supply-Trade and Commerce repeated offences. Another break-down might be the number of traffic offences involving liquor, and how many accidents involve more than one automobile.
1 would like to recommend this to the minister because I feel this problem will have to be considered either in this house or in conjunction with the various provincial legislatures, and in order to assess the problem and discuss it intelligently we will have to have a much better break-down than is provided by this department. I do not mean that as a criticism of the dominion bureau of statistics, but this important problem exists and must be faced and I think if we are to deal with it the bureau should attempt to expand its facilities in order to gather this information.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES

Mr. Chairman, I would like to draw to the minister's attention two questionnaires which are handled by the customs and immigration officials at border points. The questionnaire has its nuisance value and it irritates. The other questionnaire is directed at Canadians re-entering Canada and asks a similar question. I would say that in about 80 per cent of the cases the answers are not correct. It is not compulsory to give an answer to this question and the persons involved do not have to supply this information. I know


that in my own case on several occasions when I have been re-entering Canada and have been asked this question I have tried to answer correctly and I have later found out that I was very far short of the amount I had actually spent. speechtext: The trouble arises out of the fact that my hon. friend uses the "applications for employment" figures for purposes for which they were never intended. I saw him only two or three days ago. I said, "How are you getting on?" He said, "I like my job fine." I said, "Is your application still in at the employment office?" He said, "Oh, yes." There is no way of policing the fact whether a man who is applying for a job gets a job under his own steam or not. If they are not available, of course, their names are struck off. There is another angle, as I said; for example people who retire from the railroad. They are entitled to certain unemployment benefits. They register as available for jobs and collect their benefits as long as they last. In most cases they would not take a job if it was offered to them. Nevertheless, if they do not apply, they are not entitled to the benefits.

The position in the United States is that there is a support price for wheat. If a farmer can deliver his grain into approved storage-and there is an "if" there-and if he has not exceeded the acreage planted to wheat which he is allowed under the restriction of acreage regulations, he can borrow against that grain $2.21 a bushel. There are several "ifs" in there. As a matter of fact great quantities of free grain come on the market. They are sold by producers and are traded on the open market, and are at present selling for about $1.95 a bushel.
The millers buy their grain on the open market. They are paying about $1.95 at the present time for the grain they mill into flour, in spite of the fact that if the wheat can be put into approved storage the government will lend $2.21 on that wheat. Only


certain wheat qualifies for the loan. But if it can qualify, then as I say the farmer can borrow that amount against it. It is an irrevocable loan, and if you just walk away and leave the wheat you have your $2.21. If the price goes up you can go and redeem the wheat by paying oft the loan, and sell it for the higher price. That is the American system.
What has been the result? The result is that it has been exceedingly profitable for the big and highly mechanized farmer to produce wheat. You see plains in Texas which were never used for that purpose before, where the soil is not suitable for the growing of wheat but where, when fertilizers are used in great quantity, wheat can be grown. And they do grow wheat on those plains, and they get a very large production of a soft variety, which is not particularly suitable for merchandising. The effect of that policy is to bring in all sorts of marginal land which, on the basis of returns at market prices, would not warrant farming for wheat. That has been the effect in the United States, and we in Canada feel the brunt of that policy.
In Canada the government does not merchandise wheat. The hon. member says that the government takes away ten cents from the farmer. Well, the farmer never had that ten cents. The farmer grows the wheat and it is marketed by the wheat board. The commissioners of the wheat board are paid by the farmers, and the report is made to the farmers. The board is advised by an advisory board which contains representatives of various farm organizations, as well as representatives of the millers, and of the users of wheat. The board is a farmer organization created to market the farmers' wheat *-and to market it to whom? To market it to everybody.
The government enters the picture when it provides financing for the wheat marketing operation. At the moment the government is guaranteeing something over a hundred million dollars in bank loans to the wheat board. It also does its best to find markets for wheat, and to create trade policies to enable markets to be found for the wheat. And, as I say, we are successful, in that, in every market of which I am aware, we have sold at least our usual proportion of the market. The difficulty is that this year, as a result of a good crop in Europe and the using up of reserve stocks, the total amount of wheat going into international trade is very much less than it has been for several years.
When the hon. member says that the government takes ten cents from the farmer he should keep in mind that the government

does not market wheat at all. The government does not have anything to do with it. It is the farmers themselves who are marketing their wheat produced in western Canada. I hope my hon. friend understands what I have said, although it may be too much to expect. But I hope he will not say again that the government is taking ten cents away from the farmers.

I have listened to the debate which has taken place in the last two days. I hope this is not a repetition of the old familiar music that preceded what happened after 1930 in the Dominion of Canada.
On every hand we have an abundance of everything. People want to work, and they are willing to pay. They are willing to give service for what they receive. During the war we spent hundreds of millions of dollars for munitions. Today we have an abundance of wheat we do not know how to dispose of. The province of Ontario is teeming with foodstuffs in all the fields, east, north and south. Our cattle are standing up to their knees in lush pasture. Beef prices have dropped by 35 per cent. People are unemployed across Canada. The shipyards at Collingwood and at Midland are virtually closed down. What is the cause of all this?
Let us pray to God that what we are seeing now is not a repetition of the thirties. Let the Canadian people dispose of their heavy surplus, rather than let it rot and deteriorate. We threw our munitions away; we got rid of them, and put them to the use we thought was proper. Let us give some of our surplus away to a starving world. Let smiles come to the faces of Canadians when they think of their action in disposing of their surplus. Let them do something of which they can be justly proud. There are people who need these foods we have in such abundance.
Our trouble in Canada is that of getting rid of what we produce. How the communists must smile when they look west of the iron curtain to the North American continent! Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend is entirely confused. The present policy at ports is covered by legislation as provided in the Canadian Wheat Board Act. It provides that the initial price for the delivery of grain at Fort William, Port Arthur, Vancouver, and Churchill will be the same. That covers the price on the delivery of the farmers' grain to the ports only. There has never been a policy of selling at the same price out of these ports. Those selling prices have always been different and the difference has been the amount the traffic would bear and it relates to the competitive price of wheat out of these ports.
At the time we revised the wheat price there was a premium of ten cents per bushel on barley out of Pacific coast ports, and whenever Churchill opened we got a very substantial premium on wheat out of the port of Churchill. Usually we made an adjustment on wheat when a premium was warranted and we would hold the price at Fort William and put a premium on at Vancouver. Since we had been selling heavily out of Vancouver which is a port where grain can be handled for transit for a much longer period, we did not think the condition of the market was such that it would warrant putting a premium on at Vancouver and charging that premium on the sale of wheat to Japan and South American countries.
We felt that the demands of the market were such that a cut in price at Fort William, holding the Vancouver price steady, would be the best way to make an adjustment, rather than to hold the price at Fort William

Supply-Trade and Commerce and put a premium on the grain out of Vancouver, although one is much the same as the other.
I know of no continued policy for the selling price of wheat out of these various ports in Canada on a uniform basis. I know that the delivery price of the farmers' grain to these ports is uniform. That is provided in the wheat board act. But certainly the same shipping price out of these ports is not warranted. Let us suppose that we make Vancouver the only port and say that Fort William and Port Arthur are obsolete, and we move all the wheat through Vancouver. What would be the effect on the producers? At the present time the producer in Regina is paid an initial price of $1.40 less freight to Fort William. If Fort William was closed he would be paid the initial price less the freight to Vancouver, which would be a very much larger deduction. Now, let us take the situation at Winnipeg. The initial price there would be $1.40 less freight to Vancouver, which would certainly eat up the 40 cents and probably a bit more. We are accepting eastern grain at Vancouver at the present time to relieve congestion, but normally we cannot accept grain at Regina for shipment to Vancouver at a price based on the Fort William delivery of $1.40 less freight. We cannot accept grain on the basis of Fort William and then ship that grain to Vancouver at a very much higher freight rate. It may be good for the producer at Vancouver but it certainly is not good for the producers as a whole to sell grain at a price that is not warranted by the physical facts.
My hon. friend will therefore see that the only practical way in which to market wheat in Canada is to use all the ports based on the greater return given to the farmer and to prevent that return being swallowed up in freight rates. It is necessary to keep the ports competitive. They always have been kept competitive and they cannot operate otherwise. As long as we have a condition in this country under which it is to the advantage of the buyers abroad to buy all the grain out of one port, then we will have to sell all the grain out of one port and be prepared to make uneconomic hauls inside Canada. There is an extraordinary situation this year and because of that the people of Vancouver are complaining they are being discriminated against, but they have handled 25 per cent more grain through their port than ever before in history. If that constitutes discrimination, then it is a very strange form, and if I were a Vancouverite I would hope that that kind of discrimination would continue.

I listened with a good deal of interest to what the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra had to say, and I have also followed this matter with interest for a good number of months now. I am afraid that to the people of British Columbia this issue will still be about as clear as mud. It is as muddy as are the waters in many of the eastern Canadian rivers. We have a great deal of

respect for our responsible elected public officials at home, and when city councils, aldermen and so on express their opinion that this is a measure of discrimination we have to pay a good deal of attention to them. I regret that the reply we have thus far received has not convinced me, and I am sure has not convinced British Columbia, that this is not a measure of discrimination.
It is very well known from one end of Canada to the other that the most expensive way of moving Canadian wheat to world markets is via the great lakes route. The hon. member for Fort William assured us a while ago that all this would be taken care of after the St. Lawrence seaway was built.
Many of us out west are really wondering whether this is a measure designed to tide over eastern shipping interests until the great St. Lawrence seaway is completed. Over the past number of years we have seen a reduction in the ocean-going rate. The farmer of the west fought a long and hard battle to find an alternative route by way of Hudson bay, and then saw the efforts of the government directed towards not using these money-saving facilities. When world events and conditions now make it less costly to ship our grain through west coast ports to the markets of the world, again the government hand moves and uses its influence and power to force grain to go by the more expensive eastern route. The people of western Canada are not going to be satisfied until they receive a clear explanation. I sincerely hope the minister will be able to make a much clearer public statement.
I may be dumb, but I do know that the city council of Vancouver is not dumb. The city council of Vancouver has publicly stated that in their opinion this is a measure of discrimination against the shipping facilities that now exist on the west coast.

Is the minister going to make a statement now or later?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, it was not my intention to make any statement at this stage of the proceedings.

Mr. Chairman, I have been sitting here waiting for these estimates and it has been a long, long, day waiting for them to come. I think we are all pleased that there is a change in the consideration of the estimates. I have nothing against the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but it does seem to me we have discussed wheat for practically 50 per cent of the time. I have heard about the price of wheat, storage of wheat, the sale of wheat, and what ports it will sell from, at least four or five times, and it becomes rather boring when you hear it about the fifth time. One of the sad features about the whole thing is that I do not think all the discussion has helped to arrange for the storing of one bushel or even the sale of one bushel of wheat.
Getting back to the estimates on veterans affairs, I am a little disappointed that the minister has not seen fit to give us a general statement on veterans affairs on this first item, though I know that as the discussion continues and as we deal with the different items we will probably get all the information we require.
Besides, Mr. Chairman, we have already had a committee on veterans affairs and in that committee and in the different bills which have been before the house there has been quite a discussion already on the different phases of veterans affairs. With regard to the committee, Mr. Chairman, I might say that we are all very pleased that there was a committee set up this session. The minister and other hon. members will recall that we asked for the setting up of a special committee on veterans affairs at the beginning of the session.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
On numerous occasions we have also requested that a standing committee on veterans affairs be set up. It is nice to sit on the veterans affairs committee. You meet not only members with whom you have been associated on former veterans affairs committees, but also new members and, more particularly, you again meet the representatives of the different veterans organizations and you hear about the problems of the veterans from one end of the country to the other. You also meet the officials from the different departments and through them you get a very good picture of the situation as far as veterans problems are concerned.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, when the committee was first set up we were very much disappointed with the terms of reference as far as that committee was concerned, and at that time we tried to have the terms of reference enlarged. Most of us who sat on committees in 1945 and 1946 remember how broad the terms of reference were at that time. We could discuss practically any and all problems relating to veterans affairs. Since 1946 our terms of reference have been much more restricted, until now it hardly seems to be a veterans affairs committee at all. We are restrained from discussing some of the main problems affecting veterans and we are told that practically our only duty on the committee is to review such legislation as the government may see fit to send to us. This is something which rather irritates, indeed exasperates, the members of the committee, but I will have more to say about that matter later.
We are now considering the estimates of this department. I do not think there was ever any great objection to the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs. The only criticism that we have seen to what is being paid out to veterans in the matter of pensions, war veterans allowance and hospitalization and under the Veterans Land Act is not as to the amount. There has never been any objection to the amount but sometimes there is objection to what we think is the cost of administration. Even to that there has never been any great objection. The attitude of the members has, in my opinion, reflected the feeling or the opinion throughout the country, namely, that all we do or all the money we spend with regard to veterans affairs or for the veterans of this country is money well spent. I do not think there has ever been in this country a feeling that too much has been done for the veterans of Canada who, on two occasions, made great sacrifices not only for their own

homes but for the homes of the people of this country and of those living in other democratic countries.
We have often heard the statement made- although I think those who make it have probably never really made a study of the veterans legislation in other countries-that the legislation in Canada is the best in the world. This statement is glibly made in the House of Commons by members who, I venture to say, have never even read the legislation of the United States, for instance, or that of Australia, New Zealand or some of these other countries.
A few years ago I had the opportunity of reviewing the legislation in the United States and also some of the legislation in Australia. While our legislation compares favourably- in some matters it is better and in some it is not as good-I would doubt whether the people in the United States would agree that we in Canada have the best legislation. It is a matter of comparison. Then again, why should not Canada have the best legislation? Why should not Canada, for instance, have much better legislation for veterans than have countries like Great Britain, France, Belgium; Holland, Italy or any of those old countries?
Canada during the last war particularly did not suffer as did any of those old countries. France was devastated. Great Britain's cities and towns were ruined, and she spent practically all her finances in order to carry on the war. The same thing is true of Italy, Germany, Japan and all these other countries. In contrast, we here in Canada in no way suffered any of these tragedies, such as the destruction of our cities, our means of communication, transport and so on, as did these other countries. I therefore contend, Mr. Chairman, that the only countries with which we could make a comparison are such countries as the United States, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, which countries were not devastated as were the old countries of Europe and Asia.
With regard to paraplegics, for instance, I noticed the other day a statement to the effect that in the United States they receive something like $340 a month and are also provided with a car. Then a few months ago I noticed an article in some magazine with regard to old soldiers' homes in Australia. Here in this country we have a few old soldiers' homes, but I do not think we have anything that can compare with the old soldiers' homes in Australia or with the way in which the Australians are looking after their old veterans in that connection.

As to the matter of pensions, I suppose we have pensions comparable with those provided in any other country, but what has been the basis for the setting of the rate of pensions in this country? It has not been the highest salaries paid; not by any manner of means. We do not expect it should be and the veterans do not expect that it should be. It has not been the average salary. We all know that the pensions in this country were based on the salaries or wages which labour was receiving in this country, and those of the unskilled and cheapest labour at that. As to the young man who had left college, school, farm and so on and who went to war, if they were killed their families receive pensions; but the amount they receive would not in any way compare with the provision which would have been made for the wives and children of these men had they not been killed. The same thing applies with regard to the men who were wounded and maimed. We speak about their receiving a 100 per cent pension. What is the amount of a 100 per cent pension? I think it is $125 a month. The cheapest labour in this country today will receive $125 a month.
I am not mentioning these things, Mr. Chairman, in order to belittle our system in this country. I do so just to point out that, when we hear people say that we have the finest veterans legislation in the world, we should not take the statement too literally but should warn our people that they must not be too smug in this matter. Suppose we had the best legislation in the world. That is not the only consideration. I think that what we should give to our veterans is the best that we can afford to give them. The provision we make should not be based on what is done in other countries, but rather it should be the best that we can afford to give in this country. In that connection I should like to state that our veterans and veterans organizations in this country have always been fair in their demands. I have been amazed and well pleased at the moderate demands made by veterans when they come before veterans affairs committees. After the first war and even after the recent one, the veterans of Canada never tried to raid the treasury of this country, as was done by veterans in another country which I could mention.
We also speak of hospitalization. As far as veterans are concerned, the hospitalization in Canada is good. There has been an evolution. But again I ask this question: Should it not be good and should it not be the very best we can give? These young men were maimed and wounded not for the benefit of themselves but rather for the benefit
Supply-Veterans Affairs of this country. Many of them since the first war and now the second war have had to spend all their days in hospital. I remember, when I was in England after the first war, visiting a hospital in the southern part of that country. In the wards of this hospital were some 25 or 30 young men on water beds. I was told by the nurses there that those young men would never be moved off the beds they were on at that time. There are thousands of our young men in hospital who have been there since the first war and who will be there for the rest of their lives; and that statement now applies with regard to young men who were in the second war. I therefore say that in the matter of hospitalization, while we are proud of our institutions, there is every reason why the very best should be given to these men.
It is not my intention at this time to discuss the bills that were referred to the veterans affairs committee. They were thoroughly discussed in the committee and in the house. The committee considered Bill No. 82, having to do with the War Service Grants Act, Bill No. 101, which gave the Korean veterans the same benefits as those extended to veterans of world war II, amendments to the Pension Act and amendments to the Veterans Land Act. In my opinion the most important bill which the committee had before it was that dealing with the Veterans Land Act.
We realize that housing for veterans is one of the big problems in Canada today. I was favourably impressed with the officials who administer the Veterans Land Act and who gave evidence before the veterans affairs committee. I was impressed with their earnestness and sincerity and what I believe to be their great desire to help veterans through the Veterans Land Act and to make the new amendments a success so far as housing is concerned.
I come now to a matter which was a great disappointment as far as many members of this committee, in fact I think all, were concerned. I think I can say that all members of the house were greatly disappointed that no amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act were presented for consideration by the veterans affairs committee. As far as I am concerned, when I understood the committee would be set up I thought that the main problem which would come before it would be the matter of the war veterans allowance. It is not necessary for me to go into the history of war veterans allowances. The pages of Hansard for the past twenty-four years are filled with the history of this legislation, one of the finest acts that we have in our veterans legislation.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
But it was felt by members that the legislation had not kept pace with the requirements of veterans allowance recipients. I would say that 75 per cent of the letters members of parliament receive and 75 per cent of the complaints received from veterans organizations throughout the country arise as the result of inadequacies in the War Veterans Allowance Act. There are two great weaknesses. The first is the basic rate which today is $50 for a single man and $90 for a married man. The second great weakness is the ceiling on income or the amount of permissive income.
The War Veterans Allowance Act was considered by the veterans affairs committee of 1952, and we were surprised that these problems were not definitely solved at that time. True, the war veterans allowance was increased by $10 but the ceiling on income was reduced instead of being increased. Many hours were spent in the committee considering the matter. Many representations were made by veterans organizations pointing out these two great weaknesses in the War Veterans Allowance Act. Since that time they have increased instead of decreasing. After two years, when a veterans affairs committee is again set up for the express purpose, we thought, of reviewing and solving the problems of veterans, nothing is done respecting the problem which I and veterans throughout the country consider the most important.
The members who were on the 1952 committee will recall that at that time the Canadian Legion and every other organization strenuously objected to the bill then being considered. They pointed out that the basic rate did not even provide a bare subsistence for these older men who are unable to work and have no other means of support. They pointed out that $50 a month was not even sufficient to meet their barest requirements. As far as the ceiling on income of $120 a year is concerned, it meant that the veteran who had a small pension could not receive his pension and the benefit of the war veterans allowance. It did not permit the retired workman who had a small annuity to have the advantage of his annuity as well as the war veterans allowance. It did not even permit the war veteran recipient with two or three spare rooms in his house to rent those rooms and receive compensation for them in order to assist in meeting the expenses of the home. It did not even permit the man who had a small piece of ground in the country or near a town to take advantage of his garden or his few cows or hens without having some reduction made in his war veterans allowance.

I say that this ceiling has worked and is
working today great hardship on the war veterans allowance recipient. In the special committee this year we heard again the evidence of the representatives of the different veterans organizations. Having in mind the many letters that we are continuously receiving from veterans all over the country and the personal knowledge which I venture to say every member of the house has, having in mind the original intention of the War Veterans Allowance Act which was to assist men over 60 years of age who on account of war service were pre-aged some ten years, taking into consideration also the advanced age of these men of the first war, their average age today being 64 or 65, some of us who were members of the committee felt that we should make representations to the house asking that the terms of reference of the committee be enlarged so that this matter might be considered, especially when we saw that no bill was forthcoming from the government.
I took the opportunity to move the following motion in the special committee and I should like to read it now. It reads as follows:
That this committee submit a report to the house requesting that the terms of reference of the committee be enlarged to enable it to consider the War Veterans Allowance Act and make recommendations in respect thereof, at this session of parliament.
After considerable debate in the veterans affairs committee the chairman of that committee, for whom I have a very kind regard on all occasions but this, I am satisfied went out of his way to make what I consider a very unfair, illegal and unjust ruling, as far as this-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I think the hon. member will be able to make his point quite satisfactorily without casting reflections upon the conduct of the committee.

I am giving my opinion, Mr. Chairman. I will say this. He gave a ruling which I feel was unjustified and which, if the rules were properly carried out, cannot be justified. He gave a ruling entirely contrary to a ruling that has been made under similar circumstances in a previous committee in 1951, when we had terms of reference almost identical with those which we had in 1954. At that time a study of the War Veterans Allowance Act was permitted, although that was not in the terms of reference. The only difference between the terms of reference in 1951 and in 1954 was that in 1951 there was included an item from the estimates. The chairman said that because there was this difference in 1951, the statement of the chairman in 1951 was correct for

the particular terms of reference at that time, but would not apply to the terms of reference in 1954. As I say, there was no difference-
The hon. member was not there. I pointed out also that the terms of reference in 1951 also conferred the power to make recommendations which our terms of reference did not include.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Perhaps it might be advisable if I were to point out to the committee at this time that what is under discussion is the departmental administration of the Department of Veterans Affairs, and not the conduct of a select committee of this house. The last thing I want to do is to endeavour to curtail any fair criticism any member may wish to bring about veterans legislation, existent or non-existent. I am going to ask him to do that without criticism of the conducting of a select committee set up by this house, and particularly of the conduct of the chairman of that committee.

Surely you are not ruling that we cannot discuss the proceedings of a committee that has made a report to the house. This committee dealt with veterans affairs and a report has been brought in and tabled concerning certain recommendations. The proceedings are all printed.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra must have misunderstood me. I did not make the suggestion that the proceedings of the committee could not be discussed. I referred in particular to existent and non-existent legislation, which is the point the hon. member is now making. The manner of the conduct of a select committee of this house, not its findings but its conducting by its chairman, can only be discussed in this house on a substantive motion. That is not a question of departmental administration. I feel the hon. member whom I interrupted realizes quite well the point I am trying to make, and will see that I am not endeavouring in any way to interfere with the course of his argument. 1 am just endeavouring to head him off, before perhaps we might find we have overstepped the rules.

This is important because we all have a right to speak on this first item. I submit to you we have a right to discuss what took place in a committee. The reports are available, and every word is printed. Surely Your Honour is not ruling that we cannot refer to these printed reports.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: No, I am not.

May I finish?
Supply-Veterans Affairs

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I say he cannot discuss the conducting of the committee or criticize the conduct of the chairman of the committee on the estimates.

That is not what the hon.
member was doing. He was dealing with actions taken by the committee. Surely he is quite in order in doing that.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I think the hon. member for Royal realizes the point I was endeavouring to make.

I have heard a good many committees discussed during the discussion of the estimates, -the agriculture committee and other committees. I was suggesting that we felt the war veterans allowance should have been discussed. I feel that we made every effort we could to have the terms of reference of the committee enlarged so the matter could be discussed. We felt the war veterans allowance was the main problem that should have been before the committee. As I say, that resolution came before the committee and was ruled out of order. I shall make no further comment upon the chairman's ruling.
The veterans affairs committee submitted a report to show that the members felt that the consideration of war veterans allowances was probably the most important matter that should have been considered. In one paragraph of the report they said that, in addition to representations in respect to the said bills, representations respecting changes in the War Veterans Allowance Act, to raise the amount of allowance possible thereunder and also raise the level of permissive income, should be made. We felt also that that was not sufficient, and we had good reason for so thinking. In 1952, after certain motions were turned down in committee, we expressed the pious hope that is expressed in this report that the war veterans allowances would be considered by the government. The matter has not been considered for two years, and the same recommendation was made two years ago, yet there is still nothing done. We felt that to make such a recommendation now was no assurance either to us or to the veterans that anything would be done.
Hon. members may say, why the great hurry? As I pointed out, the recipients of the war veterans allowance are not yotmg men. Today the average age is between 64 and 65. These men are growing older every day, and they are dying off very quickly. A month or a year or two years means a great deal to them. Anyone who reads the Legionary, as I am sure most do, knows that there is a page called the "Last Post". On that

Supply-Veterans Affairs page you can see dozens of names every month of men, between the ages of 64 and 68, who have died. Brigadier Melville, the chairman of the pension commission, told us that the death rate of the veterans was increasing very rapidly. He was amazed by the great number of widows who were applying for pension. We were told also that the paraplegics of the first war have all passed on, that none of them is remaining. So I say we felt that in pressing for this to be done now- not a year or two years hence-we were carrying out what we believed were the wishes of veterans bodies, and also what should be done to give justice to these veterans. In this connection I should like to read a paragraph from the Legion brief of May 19, 1954:
It is the earnest hope of the Canadian Legion that the present committee will realize the need and assume the responsibility of recommending immediate action in this matter.
And the matter concerning which they ask for immediate action is that of war veterans allowances. I am not going to labour the point further. I do not think it is necessary to do so; but by failing to enlarge the terms of reference of our committee and failing to allow us to consider a bill amending the war veterans allowances, I feel a great injustice has been done by parliament so far as the recipients of war veterans allowances are concerned. I express the hope that between now and next November the government will see fit to correct this great injustice. And if it is not done at that time, then one of the first things we will have to do at the next session of parliament will be to discuss the War Veterans Allowance Act.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Why not do it before this session ends?

Mr. Chairman, I shall take a few minutes on this first item, because it is about the only place I can say what I want to say.
Two principles arise out of the last veterans affairs committee that should be brought home clearly to members of the House of Commons. The first of these is the value of the committee itself, and the second is this warning: Don't tie the hands of the committee before you set it up.
Ever since I have been in the House of Commons I have been of the opinion that a continuing committee on veterans affairs, operating as a standing committee of the house, would serve a very useful purpose. It could review and consider week by week or month by month, in company with representatives seeking veterans legislation, what might be wrong with the present legislation


and what new legislation might be required. In this way there could be a continuous survey of veterans problems.
While it was handicapped in one respect, this committee demonstrated that when its hands were not tied by previous decisions it was flexible and realistic and could do some good work. I shall not discuss the four bills which came before the house more than to say that the committee made amendments to those bills simply because it was not hamstrung before it began its sittings.
For example, under the War Service Grants Act veterans who served in Korea and had enlisted prior to 1950 found, upon being discharged, that they were not entitled to unemployment insurance. Through the chairman and the parliamentary assistant this matter was brought to the attention of the committee. The proposal was a reasonable one and it was not long before the parliamentary assistant had consulted his minister and others and returned to the committee with an amendment correcting this injustice.
Then there was another amendment to the same act in connection with which we were not hamstrung by previous decisions. I refer to the application of gratuity credits to dependent parents. When the matter was discussed in committee the act was changed from a provision whereby the parent had to be wholly supported by the deceased veteran to one whereby only partial support was necessary. I know of several cases in which I was interested where the difficulty was cured by this amendment.
When the Veterans Land Act came before the committee it was amended in 15 places. This shows that if the committee is permitted to work without restriction it can and will do a good job. In this connection I should like to straighten out something that appeared in a newspaper report dealing with the first principle I stated when I stood in my place: Don't tie the hands of the committee before you set it up. This report appears in the Ottawa Citizen of Friday, June 11, 1954, at page 5. It is a Canadian Press dispatch and while I do not know who wrote it, I am certain no one in the parliamentary press gallery wrote the headline, which states "Second Veto for Raise in Vets Pensions". That headline is absolutely incorrect. Then I shall refer to the first paragraph of the dispatch which, also, is in error. It states:
For the second time in two days, Walter Tucker (Liberal, Rosthern), chairman of the Commons veterans affairs committee, yesterday ruled out of order a motion aimed at increasing war veterans allowances.

The paragraph is in error when it states the motion was to increase war veterans allowances. It was for a completely different purpose, that of asking the committee to broaden the terms of reference.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Asking the house.

To ask the house to broaden the terms of reference. The rest of the story is all right. Then, I should like to say a few words on the other principle: Don't tie the hands of the committee. The matter of broadening the terms of reference was raised by the hon. member for Royal. As he said this afternoon, the committee had before it a proposal from the chairman to write into its report a recommendation that the government give greater consideration to war veterans allowances in respect of those who served in the merchant marine during the last war. Under his authority the chairman was not permitted to accept the motion of the hon. member for Royal. I have served on that committee long enough to know the rules.
However, he found himself in this position; a much less favourable one. Before the matter came to the committee at all, the Legion had approached the cabinet, and the cabinet is the government. It was indicated in the press that the cabinet, with the Prime Minister as its spokesman, had definitely said there was to be no change in war veterans allowances at this session of the house. That was a pretty definite government decision.
On two occasions the house had ruled out of order a proposal to broaden the terms of reference of the committee when the matter was under discussion. I like to be fair in these matters. In what kind of a position did we place the members of the government who were members of that committee, in deciding to broaden the terms of reference or increasing veterans' allowances, when three decisions against that proposal had already been made; one by the cabinet and two by the house before the committee had an opportunity of discussing it at all? From my own experience on that committee in the last fifteen years I am reasonably sure that if that committee gets any proposition, and if they are not hamstrung before they start, they will do a reasonable job in the best interests of the veterans of this country.
In the committee, as I stated when the hon. member for Royal moved his motion, the easy thing for an opposition member to do is to rise and beat the chairman, because the chairman is helpless. He has no alternative. He goes as far as he can under the
Supply-Veterans Affairs rules and regulations that apply to that committee. There is no doubt in my mind- and there was no doubt in my mind-that the hon. member for Royal was out of order.
That is not the attitude you took in former veterans committees.
But the circumstances were different this time. Three decisions had been made by the government and hon. members. That is what I am objecting to.
No decision was made on this.
There were two decisions made.
Not on this.

Two of them were made in this house and one was made by the government as announced by the Prime Minister to the Legion. I hope we have learned a lesson from that, so that when we set up that committee we set it up free to deal with veterans problems, without having three strikes on it before it starts to discuss the proposition. I have said that a good many times and I reiterate it now. Let us not get the committee in a position where people are fighting for the political advantages. Let us set it up free and unrestricted, and let us not examine legislation that has been conceived by someone else. Let us look at the legislation as it is and let us, along with veterans organizations, determine what is fair and reasonable in the matter of changes to be made. Then I think we can keep veterans affairs out of politics and the veterans will get a better deal all-round.
There are lots of places where I can fight politically with the government, in the house and out of the house, but there is one problem in this country that I have never for one minute tried to capitalize on politically, and that is veterans affairs. It should be outside of that; it is too big for that.
I do not forget the 1951 and 1952 committees when the War Veterans Allowance Act was before them. The main emphasis at that time was on permissible earnings, casual earnings; the right of the veteran to hold his veterans allowance and at the same time take some employment that would increase his income and enable him to augment the veterans allowance, instead of immobilizing and penalizing him if he took employment of any kind. I do not agree with the hon. member for Royal when he says nothing was done about that other than expressing a pious hope. At that time the main emphasis was on casual earnings. He will remember, as I remember-

The main emphasis was on the ceiling, and it is today.

Supply-Veterans Affairs

It is the same; there is no difference. It is a difference in words. At that time the department dug out material as far back as 1919, and we gave that problem a thorough overhauling. I hold in my hand directive No. 25, issued in 1953, which shows that substantial changes were made in the casual earnings and in the methods of going off veterans allowances, taking employment for part of the year and going back on the allowance again without any difficulty. I am not going to read it. I am sure every member of the veterans affairs committee must have a copy of this directive. Substantial changes were made.
Previous to the changes being made, as indicated in the directive, I received many letters on this matter of casual earnings, asking that the ceiling be raised and wondering why they were immobilized, asking that they be permitted to take employment for a month, two months or three months of the year, and so on. They said, "if I take a little job on an elevator or selling tickets at a theatre, or some kind of employment that a person can get in the summertime, why should I be deprived of my veterans allowance?" I have had no complaints since that was straightened out in accordance with the directive. Then the main issue became that of raising the basic rates.
As far as I am concerned, if we had a chance to discuss and vote on that, there would be no question where I stand. I am sure there is no doubt in anybody's mind, in this house or outside of it, who knows me as to where I would stand on that matter; but that matter was not before us and we could not get it before us. We were prevented from getting it before us largely by the action of this house in making two decisions against it before it ever got to us.
I have another directive in my hand which is along the same lines. It has to do with casual earnings as they apply to farmers in the computation of their income. I am not going to read it because it is available to all hon. members. It is the issue of May 3, 1954, and is directive No. 6. It is worth having in your file. Anyone who is interested in veterans affairs should have both of these directives in his files. These directives are all supposed to go out to the district offices, which are responsible for advising the veterans in the district, but quite often this material gets sidetracked. When I saw this I suggested in the house that revisions should be made so that the branches and people in the area at least would become familiar with it.

These are some of the things that that committee did. I am arguing for that committee. I am not defending the government, but I am arguing as to the value of that committee. I am sure the hon. member for Royal did not mean what might be taken out of his remarks if you did not know him: a straight condemnation of a committee of this house by a man who has been a member of it for some considerable time. He said that it is of no value and that instead of setting it up as a continuing committee as a lot of us want to see done, the government should say: let us get rid of it; it is no good anyway, since some of the older members have said so.
I never said that.

I know the hon. member did not say that, but that could be read out of what he said; that it is of no value; that it only issues pious hopes; that it has not done anything and it has never done anything; why should we be wasting our time? If I ever get the idea that the committee is a waste of time, I will not be a member of it. I will not be wasting my time on it. I consider it one of the most valuable committees in the House of Commons.
If it is not hamstrung.

If it is not hamstrung. Let us not help to hamstring it the next time by voting on something in this house that we should do in the committee.
While I am talking about veterans allowances I would like to say this to the minister. There are two points about veterans allowances that would not take very much money to straighten out, and they are outstanding grievances. One is the veteran who served in England during the first world war. That veteran should be entitled to war veterans allowances. England was not a theatre of war during the first war; it was a theatre of war in the second war. A veteran who served in the second war and who got to England, and who may be 30 or 35 years of age, may some day receive veterans allowances. The man who served in England and stayed in England through no fault of his own, because he was ordered to stay there, sees, when he reaches the age of 60 or 65, the young veterans drawing allowances to which he himself should be entitled. He feels it is a pretty rank piece of discrimination. I say that something should be done to correct that.
Now, the second point, and this is an outstanding grievance, relates to the widow of the imperial veteran. With the deadline of 20 years residence there were many of them who were perhaps three, five, or eight months

short of being residents in Canada for the regulation 20 years. That widow is living alongside Mrs. Smith who was lucky enough to have a husband who lived in Canada for the full 20 years and who therefore receives the full war veterans allowance. But the woman next door, because her husband happened to be taken away a few months before, does not qualify under that deadline and she cannot get the war veterans allowance.
There would not be very much money involved in alleviating the condition of such people. When you talk to people in that category and tell them you are in favour of putting $100 million into the Colombo plan they come right back and say, "Why not start a Colombo plan for us?" The amount of money involved would not be so great when one considers that this is really an outstanding grievance.
I would suggest that when the government considers the report of the committee, which suggests that the war veterans allowance should be considered in the matter of increasing the rate, that these two points I have just mentioned, both of which are outstanding grievances, be given further consideration. That is all I am going to say at the present time, Mr. Chairman, but I may have some further remarks to make on certain other items.

Mr. Chairman, when the veterans charter was first introduced in 1945 I believe it was the finest program for the re-establishment of veterans that could be found in any country in the world.
