As time went on, of course, it became necessary to make adjustments to that charter and for that purpose the veterans committee has been set up to deal with the amendments and bills referred to it from time to time. In the early days the terms of reference of that committee were wide open and we had the right to discuss any feature of the veterans charter but, unfortunately, during the past few years the terms of reference have been tightened up and our action has been limited to the bills referred to us. As a result of that it has not been possible for the committee to deal with what might be considered the major grievances in the veterans charter and that, of course, is the war veterans allowance.
I want to deal with one or two of the bills which were referred to the committee and deal first of all with the Veterans' Land Act. When the Veterans' Land Act was before the house I suggested to the minister that the superintendent should be prepared to give us a complete review of the operations of the department. At this time I would like to commend the very fine report that was given
Supply-Veterans Affairs to the committee by the superintendent of the Veterans' Land Act. It was a very comprehensive report; it showed that the program is working, I think, very satisfactorily; and it showed there are very few veterans in arrears. I think at the same time we must keep in mind the fact that generally speaking crops have been good and prices have been satisfactory. It is quite possible that if we run into a few crop failures and prices happen to fall the situation might not be quite so satisfactory.
The main criticism I have heard of the officials of the Veterans' Land Act has been that they have been a little bit too tough; that they are a bit too conservative in their appraisals. The superintendent himself admitted before the committee that there is probably some justification for that criticism. On the other hand, I would not be too critical of the superintendent on that ground because I have in mind the criticisms we have made throughout the past about the officials of the old Soldier Settlement Act. That was constantly criticized on the grounds that the settled veterans were put on land for which they had to pay too high a price, and that they should never have settled veterans on land of that type. I presume that the present superintendent is going to try and make sure that that type of criticism will never be levelled against him in the future.
Now, one of the amendments under the act provided for an additional loan of $3,000 which I think is a good thing. On the other hand, I regret that the government set the rate of interest at 5 per cent instead of 3J per cent. I hope the government even at this late date will reconsider that action. The reason given was that the main purpose of the additional loan was to make it possible for the veterans to get loans they were not able to get as veterans under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, and as the rate of interest was 5 per cent under the Farm Improvement Loans Act the rate of interest for this additional $3,000 should also be set at 5 per cent.
But that ignores one very important fact, namely, that the Veterans' Land Act has nothing whatever to do with the Farm Improvement Loans Act. It also ignores the fact that when the Veterans' Land Act was established and the veterans came back from overseas many of them were encouraged and advised by the officials of the Veterans' Land Act not to settle right away but to wait. Prices were high and they were advised to hold back in the hope that the prices would fall and they would be able to make a better deal with their $6,000. But what happened?

Supply-Veterans Affairs Prices went up by about 50 or 60 per cent and as a consequence of the veteran having taken the advice of the officials of the Veterans' Land Act-and I am not criticizing these officials because most of us thought the same thing-the veteran found himself in a far more difficult position. Whereas with his $6,000 he might have been able to settle on a good holding in 1943, 1944 or 1945, by 1947, 1948, 1949 and onwards, the price of land had gone up by 50 per cent and in some cases 100 per cent, along with the price of everything else, and so it was practically impossible for the veteran to become re-established with $6,000. In most cases the veterans who did manage to become re-established had a certain amount of capital of their own and in some cases they were helped out by their parents.
Now we find a situation in which it is desirable to make an additional amount of $3,000 available. According to the superintendent and the minister the purpose is to make it possible for the veterans to obtain additional land and improve their property. The government realized they needed to expand their holdings and with the price of land being high it had not been possible in many cases for the veteran to get a large enough holding. As a result of the price of land increasing this $6,000 was not sufficient to enable the veteran to buy a sufficient amount of land which could be considered as an economic unit. We are therefore allowing the settler to have an additional $3,000. But that being the case what justification can there be for setting the rate of interest at 5 per cent instead of 3i per cent?
This grant is being made in order to make it possible for the veterans to establish an economic unit, but I would again point out that it has nothing whatever to do with the Farm Improvement Loans Act and I therefore hope the government will give further consideration to that matter and make the rate of interest 34 per cent across the board. As things stand now we will have the veteran paying 34 per cent on some of his loan and 5 per cent on the balance.
As I said, I think the officials implementing the Veterans Land Act are doing a good job. They have a reputation today of being tough but the time to be tough is, of course, when prices and crops are good and when farmers are prosperous. If the time comes when conditions are bad I hope the minister will encourage his officials to be a little more lenient in order to make things a little easier for those in that position. I agree the time to be tough is at the beginning and then loosen up later on.

I now want to say a few words with regard to the Pension Act. A great deal of concern was expressed by the Legion in their brief over the delay in awarding pensions. It will be recalled that the act, as originally sent to the committee, instead of improving that situation, worsened it. Fortunately, the government decided to agree to an amendment to the bill and the situation was put back as it was before the bill was drafted. But it still does not go as far as the Legion asked that it should go. The Legion asked that the pension be awarded from the date of application. I hope the government will see fit to give further consideration to that matter at some future date.
I now want to come to the question of the main grievance against the veterans charter today, namely, the grievance against the war veterans allowance. There again I want to state that I am not for one moment criticizing the officials of the war veterans allowance board. I think Colonel Garneau has done a good job. I have never heard any criticism against him or his officials. I think they go as far as they can go under the act. In my opinion the trouble is that, the act being what it is, they are not able to go far enough.
There has been some criticism of the chairman of the committee for ruling a certain amendment out of order. Generally speaking, I think he made a good chairman. I think most of the members of the committee will agree with that statement. Personally I am not overcritical of him for having ruled out of order that motion to get the terms of reference widened. Even if that amendment had been allowed, it would either have been voted down by the Liberal members of the committee, or if it had not been voted down by the members of the committee, I presume it would have been voted down when it got into the house, because two amendments that had been moved at the time the committee was set up had already been voted down. While it might have been a good political move to make, I do not think it would have done much good even if it had carried in the committee.
When the War Veterans Allowance Act was before the committee in 1952 the allowance was raised from $40 a month to $50 for a single veteran and from $70 to $90 for a married veteran. But at the same time the amount of the permissible earnings of a married veteran was reduced from $250 for the year to $120. That reduction caused a great deal of hardship for the small pensioner -that is the war disability pensioner-or for the person with a small superannuation allowance or any other type of pension. What

it meant was this. A married veteran with a disability pension of $30 a month did not receive any help whatsoever as the result of increasing the war veterans allowance from $70 a month to $90 a month, because the ceiling permitted was $1,200 for a married veteran. That was my main criticism at that time, namely, that although we had increased the allowance from $70 a month to $90, it would not help the small disability pensioner in any way, shape or form.
I think the tragic part of the picture with regard to the War Veterans Allowance Act is that it does not today provide enough for a person to live on. Furthermore, it denies a veteran the right to help himself by adding money to his income in order that he may have a fairly decent standard of living. It makes it impossible for a veteran to help himself. The recipient of the war veterans allowance today is therefore forced to exist on a subsistence standard and there is nothing he can do to help it.
Not only is there nothing that the veteran can do to help himself, there is nothing that his relatives can do to help him and there is nothing that his friends can do to help him. If they start to make money available to him, then the amount of his allowance is reduced by that amount, unless the matter is hidden, unless he conceals the fact that help is being given to him. Moreover, if it becomes disclosed at a later date, the allowance is cut down and the amount of overpayment is charged against his future allowance.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Even old age security is of no help.

Yes; even old age security is of no help to him. I think all of us know of many cases of real hardship. Veterans have come to us and said that their sons and daughters wanted to help them and have asked the question: How can they help us without our having the allowance cut down? There is no way they can help unless it is done by not disclosing the fact that help is being given. Yet no member likes to encourage a recipient of war veterans allowance to do anything that is not legal because if he does so, and it is found out, of course naturally the member of parliament would be blamed for having given him a bum steer. I myself have been in that position on several occasions, but I have been discreet. I would say that the officials are very sympathetic. They use good judgment. If there is one department that bends over backward to try to help the veteran, it is the branch of the war veterans allowance.
Supply-Veterans Affairs
Another highly unsatisfactory condition is that today we find that old age pensioners in some provinces are getting a far better deal than are the recipients of the war veterans allowance. For instance, in Alberta and in British Columbia that is the situation. I do not want anybody to bring politics into the matter. It just happens that Social Credit governments are in power there. That is not the reason I am referring to the matter. I am merely mentioning that in the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia a married couple receive an old age pension of $110 a month whereas recipients of the war veterans allowance receive $90 a month. That is a rather bad situation, where a civilian can receive $20 a month more than a war veteran; therefore the war veterans allowance should be increased. Mind you, Mr. Chairman, the War Veterans Allowance Act and the Old Age Security Act are not altogether dissociated from each other. There is a connection between them, whether we like it or not.
First of all, let us remember that the war veterans allowance is not available to all disabled veterans. It is available only to those veterans who actually served in a theatre of war. Very often there is a narrow margin between a veteran who is able to get a pension and a veteran who is not able to get one and who has to accept the war veterans allowance. I can see that at times it must be an extremely difficult thing for the pension commission to decide what veteran will be able to get a pension and what veteran will have to depend upon the War Veterans Allowance Act for his living. Of course, the pension commission is allowed to use the section with regard to benefit of the doubt in order to help it in that matter. 1 can quite well see where, at times, it must be a hard decision for the pension commission to make.
In this connection it is well to remember that in the year the War Veterans Allowance Act was first established-I have forgotten the exact date, but it was in the 1930's-it was established upon the presumption that a veteran had pre-aged by ten years. I have not the statement here but I read the statement by the former prime minister to that effect. The veteran having pre-aged by ten years, it was decided to allow the veteran to have the old age pension at the age of sixty instead of waiting until he was seventy. That being the case, and the war veterans allowance having been established on that basis, what possible justification can there be for maintaining a means test upon the recipient of the war veterans allowance at sixty when the recipient of the old age pension at seventy has no means test upon him?
61EE

Supply-Veterans Affairs On that basis war veterans should automatically have the means test lifted at 60. Otherwise the presumption basis means nothing.
That could mean a great deal to the recipients of war veterans allowance because the majority of the war veterans are over 60 years of age. I have here a statement which was made by Colonel Garneau in 1952. According to that statement at that time the actual percentage of veterans under 60 years of age compared with those 60 years of age and over was in the ratio of 25 per cent to 75 per cent. The percentage with respect to widows on allowances under 55 years of age was 16-58 per cent and for those 55 years of age or over 83-42 per cent. These figures total approximately 32 per cent for those under 60 years of age and 68 per cent for those 60 years of age and over, taking in all recipients.
That would mean that if we recognize that veterans of 60 receiving the war veterans allowance should have the means test lifted entirely, 68 per cent of the recipients of the war veterans allowance would have the means test eliminated. I think all members would agree that would make a tremendous difference to the war veterans today. In the first place it would mean that all those receiving disability pensions would be able to get the full amount of the war veterans allowance. All those getting small incomes from other sources would be able to get the full amount of the war veterans allowance. I hesitate to go one step further and say that it would mean that they could also draw the full amount of the old age pension at 65. I am not going to say that because I do realize that there seems to be a duplication there, and if you are going to argue that the one is based upon the other I do not see how you can say they can get both.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Retired judges get both.
But by the time they reach 70 we should be prepared to give them both the allowance and the old age security pension which is contributory.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Retired judges get two pensions. Some senators get both their indemnities and the pension.

Yes, but I am using an argument which I will admit does not work very well in that direction. However, I believe it is a most important argument to use. First, on the basis of that presumption, the veteran at 60 is certainly entitled to have the means test lifted, and by the time he is 70 I think we could very well pay him the full amount of the old age pension and the war veterans allowance. However, I admit

I have not made a very good case for the latter although I have made an excellent case for the first proposition, namely, that the means test should be eliminated.
The Legion has not gone that far. They have not asked that the means test be eliminated entirely. They have asked that the means test be raised to the approximate level of the income tax exemptions. They suggest that the ceiling on permissive income in the case of the single veteran should be raised to $1,200 and the ceiling on permissive income in the case of the married veteran should be raised to $2,000. The justification for that of course is that when that exemption was established under the income tax it was established on the basis that a person with an income of less than that could not live on less and therefore should not be taxed. For the same reason, if a single man cannot live on less than $1,200 a year and a married man cannot live on less than $2,000 a year, then the ceilings on income should be raised to those amounts in order to make it possible for the veteran to live a decent life. No veteran can live a decent existence under the miserable ceiling now prevailing.
I should like to draw the attention of the minister to the fact that in 1952 the committee made a recommendation regarding the war veterans allowance which reads as follows:
Your committee further recommends to the government continued and sympathetic study of the needs and requirements of recipients of war veterans allowance, keeping in mind the recommendations of veterans organizations in that respect and particularly with regard to permissive income.
This year the committee made what is in reality a similar recommendation. It asked the government to give sympathetic consideration to the recommendations of the veterans organization. I hope the minister and the government will give the matter further consideration and find it possible to go at least as far as the recommendation of the Legion, even if they are not prepared to adopt my proposal to wipe out the means test at the age of 60.

Mr. Chairman, I am glad that the last words I will be privileged to say in the house at this session will be along exactly the same line as my first words in the house, the strongest appeal I can make for some consideration for people on war veterans allowances, both with respect to the limit of the allowance and, in particular, the ceiling on permissive income. I want to take the few minutes before six o'clock to talk a bit about the work of the special committee.

I was trying to think the other day of just what we had done in this session of parliament and what we had left undone, whether I was proud of having done anything or ashamed of having done something. I was trying to total up the things that really mattered, and one small thing came to my mind. I had the privilege of writing a letter to the minister with regard to adopted children of war pensioners. I tried to use what influence I had to get him to put them on a par with natural children, and I think the greatest thrill I got at this session was to see the minister take steps a few days later to make provision for that in the law.
I hasten to add that hon. members on this and the other side of the house, who for so many years have fought so well for the veterans, no doubt suggested that long before I did, but perhaps I just happened to write at the particular time. I v/ant to pay tribute to two members of the veterans affairs committee for the work they did. In my humble opinion the finest job was done by our chairman, the hon. member for Rosthern, who did an extremely difficult job to the satisfaction of all concerned. I also got a thrill when on the last day of our sittings I heard the clerk say that we have the highest rate of attendance of any committee of the house. I admit that a good many of our sessions were pretty hot, but I think if members of the four different political parties will look back on the work that was done in that committee they will agree that we were all trying to achieve the same purposes.
We have heard today about a resolution that was ruled out of order. I have not heard anything yet about the one that was ruled out of order by the same chairman the day before, and which happened to be a resolution moved by two British Columbia Liberal members, the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard and the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond. Its purpose was to more or less implement the proposals in the Legion brief for higher war veterans allowances and a higher permissive income.
The second hon. member to whom I want to pay my tribute is the modest member for Cape Breton South. A few weeks ago I heard him make a speech on international policy which I thought was one of the most important things I had heard in the house this year. Although it did happen to be an expression of C.C.F. international policy, it was an important speech, and if I were a Russian diplomat I certainly would have paid very close attention to it because it seemed to me to be a speech coming from the heart of an honest man. The work done by the hon. member for Cape Breton South in the veterans affairs committee this year was a peace-making job.
Supply-Veterans Affairs
We were faced by a practical difficulty. The terms of reference of the veterans affairs committee were narrower than most members of the committee wished to have. I know quite well every member of that committee would have been delighted had we had before us the War Veterans Allowance Act, and had we been able to make recommendations for concrete increases in those allowances and in the ceiling on permissive income. Some hon. members may recall that I ventured to suggest when we were unsuccessful in having the terms of reference widened, that we would find ways and means of discussing the war veterans allowance. This turned out to be the case because in the debate we had over the precise form in which we were going to lend our moral support to the Legion brief I think the hon. member for Cape Breton South and the chairman, as well as one or two other members of the committee from other parties, put their heads together, and we all know what the end result was. The end result was that in the second to the last paragraph of the final report of the veterans affairs committee we gave our wholehearted support to the Legion brief and the submissions they made for increases in the war veterans allowance and a rise in the ceiling on permissive income.
I want to say also that I thought the work of the veterans affairs committee this year showed itself as very valuable. I heartily support the proposal made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South that this veterans affairs committee be made a permanent standing committee. We should not have to have it set up specially every year. I shall cite just one small example of the benefits we have this year from this committee. The hon. member for Cape Breton South discovered that there was a weakness in the Unemployment Insurance Act, in that it excluded certain categories of veterans. He took that up with the Minister of Veterans Affairs, and we all know the sequel. The sequel was the introduction of a new bill to remedy this grievance.
I must say that I go home from this session with mixed feelings. I am frankly disappointed that the government did not feel able to completely accept the recommendations of the Canadian Legion concerning war veterans allowance, and particularly in regard to their feeling on permissive income. I could not agree altogether with the hon. member for Acadia, for whom I have great respect, about that business of the old age pension. I believe that if the permissive income were not even put as high as the Legion requested, which was $1,200, if it were even set at $1,080, that would solve

Supply-Veterans Affairs the difficulty because that would amount to $40 a month. This would mean that a man could draw his $50 a month that he now draws, and when he gets to age 70 he would automatically be entitled to the old age security pension without any deduction because he would still be under the ceiling.
I want to say once again, Mr. Chairman, just as strongly as I can that I urge the minister and the government to give sympathetic consideration to the people on war veterans allowance. I say that not just because there are hundreds of them in my riding or because we have thousands of them in British Columbia. When I wake up in the morning and begin to read the newspaper and I see, for instance, that last night in some little rooming house perhaps in one corner of my riding some old worn-out exwarrior turned on the gas, I must confess I do not feel too happy. Usually, when they examine his accounts they find that he just could not get by on $50 per month. I, for one, have no hesitation whatever in saying that in the two far western provinces, Alberta and British Columbia, the fact that the old age pensioners draw $55 a month is a real source of grievance to the people who served their country in time of war and who are now forced to live on $50 a month.
Once again I urge the minister to continue to give sympathetic consideration to this proposal. I cannot state publicly that I know where the minister's sympathy lies in this regard. May I urge upon the minister and the government again, as I have so many times before, to continue to give to the war veterans allowance every sympathetic consideration. In addition to that, in the coming months they should give even extra consideration to what seems to me to be by far the most important part of this whole question, and that is the ceiling on permissive income. I have no way of knowing what was in the minds and hearts of the people who had to make a decision that this government was not able to afford an increase in veterans allowances this year. I, for one, might hazard a guess that had the Legion not asked for an over-all rise from $50 to $60 per month, but had confined their request to the more important grievance, the low limit on permissive income, perhaps we could have obtained at least one of the things which I think every hon. lady and gentleman in this house wishes as much as every other.
Since we are sitting again at seven o'clock, may I call it six o'clock?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
May I remind hon. members that pursuant to special order the committee will resume at seven o'clock this evening.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at seven o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, I should like
to make a few brief remarks on this first item in the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs. First of all I should like to compliment the minister on the veterans legislation that was put forward by the government, considered by the special committee on veterans affairs and subsequently passed.
I should like to mention particularly the amendments to the Veterans Land Act, because I think these are certainly very beneficial to the veterans who served in all fields of hostilities, and they are most commendable. I would say the same with respect to the amendments to the Pension Act, with the exception of that one section which had to do with the setting of the salaries of the commissioners. And of course I cannot refer to that at this time. In any event, on the whole the legislation referred to the special committee was commendable.
For a few moments I should like to deal with two recommendations set forth in the brief of the Canadian Legion and which thus far have not been acted upon by the government. The first item in this connection has to do with the submission by the Canadian Legion with respect to dependent parents. The fact that the government recognized that a dependent widowed mother should be placed on the same footing as a widow was recognized in the original legislation. However after 1951, when changes were made in pension rates, the pension of a widow was raised to a maximum of $100 a month from $75, whereas that of the widowed mother remained at $75. Without going into the details in the Legion's brief I would say that in my view they presented a capable argument on the point, and showed that pensions for widowed mothers of veterans should be increased at the same rate as widows' pensions were. As the principle was recognized in the first place I cannot see any logical reason for not continuing it.
The matter of war veterans allowances has been probably the most contentious in the field of veterans affairs during this session of parliament. All of us realize that the

special committee on veterans affairs had very limited responsibilities. It considered only certain legislation proposed by the government, and its activities could not extend beyond that. When the various government bills referred to this special committee were being considered evidence was heard from various veterans bodies, and from others; and inevitably, of course, the matter of war veterans allowances did creep in. My recollection is that at one time or another most members of the committee expressed the view that war veterans allowances should be increased, or that they were sympathetic toward such increases.
I agreed thoroughly with the remarks this afternoon of the hon. member for Cape Breton South when he said that the activities of this special committee should not have been hamstrung from the start, and that a standing committee on veterans affairs should be established. I hope this will be done at the next session of parliament.
However a most interesting situation arose when the hon. member for Royal, if I may coin a phrase, tried to "unhamstring" the activities of this particular committee. The hon. member made a motion which, in effect, attempted to enlarge the activities of the committee, in which he suggested that parliament be requested to change the terms of reference of the committee so that the subject of war veterans allowances could be considered. It was interesting to note that all government members on the committee as well as two members from one of the other parties to my left voted against this request.

May I ask a question? That is not right, at all. The government members voted to uphold the ruling of the chairman, who had dealt with points of order for about two hours, and gave a ruling showing how the amendment was clearly out of order. In view of the fact that we had expressed our hearty support of what the thing was supposed to be doing, I think everybody understood exactly what the score was.
The hon. member for Vancouver South said he wished to ask a question. I would like to know what his question is.
Was not the vote to which the hon. member referred a vote to uphold the ruling of the chair, and not on the substance about which the hon. member is talking.

The vote certainly was to uphold the ruling of the chair; that is true. But in effect what was being voted on was 83276-390i
Supply-Veterans Affairs a motion by the hon. member for Royal to request parliament to extend the activities of the committee. And I believe the hon. member for Vancouver South knows perfectly well that that was the effect of the motion. It is true of course that from a technical point of view we were voting to uphold or to reject the ruling of the chairman. In effect however what happened was what I have just mentioned.
In his remarks this afternoon the hon. member for Vancouver South referred to an earlier motion by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard with respect to war veterans allowances, and which members of the government party from British Columbia were prepared to support. The motion was ruled out of order at that time. The only observation I have to make is that when it was ruled out of order I failed to understand why the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard did not appeal the chairman's ruling, which he was entitled to do, and which the hon. member for Royal actually did when his motion was ruled out of order. However all these facts are available to hon. members, and I can see no point in continuing the discussion further. Everybody who reads the report of the special committee on veterans affairs can see what occurred; but I just mention this in passing. It seems strange to me that some hon. members, who I am sure were genuinely sympathetic-in fact I think most members of the committee, if not all, were generally sympathetic-to war veterans allowances, failed to act in this matter when the opportunity to do so arose.
In their brief to the government the Legion set out clearly, concisely and reasonably the reasons why they felt war veterans allowances should be raised from $50 a month to $60 a month for a single man and from $90 a month to $120 a month for a married person; and also that the ceiling on permissive income should be raised. I believe the amount suggested was from $750 to $1,200 for a single person and from $1,200 to $2,000 for a married person. It is my understanding, and I am open to correction on this by the minister, that the suggestions made by the Legion would cost about $3 million a year, which does not seem to be a very extravagant amount. I am quite sure that most citizens would not object to paying another $3 million a year to help our older burnt-out veterans.
In his budget speech this year the Minister of Finance announced that owing to certain tax reductions there would be a decrease of $36 million a year in income. Without going into details, these tax reductions were brought

Supply-Veterans Affairs about by the removal of taxes on fishing rods, golf clubs, electrical appliances, perfume, pinball machines and things of that sort. I do not think there is a citizen in Canada who would object to having taxes to the extent of $3 million remain on pinball machines, perfumes, golf clubs and so on, if some of our older veterans who are not able to support themselves could be paid the war veterans allowance. For that reason I feel that it certainly should have been considered by the government.
Of course there are many sad individual cases of people who need increases in war veterans allowances, and one could cite them at great length. To illustrate the fact that I honestly believe that war veterans allowances ought to be increased, I should like to read a section, and only a section, of a letter that I received recently. The writer of this letter is a Mrs. A. Williams who resides at rural route No. 1, Drumbo, Ontario. I shall quote only the pertinent parts of the letter. They are as follows:
There is, however, one thing of interest to me, that of the veterans allowance. As a receiver of this allowance, I would at this time like to explain, if I may be permitted a little of your time, that the general public are wrongly informed of this. A while ago great write-ups in the news that the veterans were getting an increase (331 per cent) in their pensions. This covered all pensioners whether receiving $100 or $20 pensions, this they did. Then more write-ups that the government were increasing the veterans allowance from $40 to $50 single men and from $60 to $90 for married. Naturally the public were under the impression, the vets were being exceptionally well cared for. I am just one of many, but would like to explain just how this worked in our case. In 1950 my husband, unable to work, applied for the veterans allowance. He was receiving a small pension of $28. When the inspector found that I couldn't work either, owing to a heart condition, they allowed him $66.66, which they said was the maximum, making our total $94.66 per month. In 1952 they gave the 331 per cent increase and then the increase in veterans allowance. So we receive $34 pension now and $66 veterans allowance (66 cents less veterans allowance), making now $100 per month, but where do they get a raise in veterans allowance? Naturally the public figured we received an extra $30 on top of the $60 we were already receiving, which if it really were so, would only be $130 per month. I am sure there are many others like us, and we trust this matter will soon be passed in the house, for I assure you it is most difficult to manage with taxes, insurance and living, etc., increasing and no increase in income to cover same.
Without taking up any more time, may I say I have no doubt that other examples will be cited during the remarks this evening. I should like to mention one further matter. I am sure the government is aware of the fact that most of the recipients of war veterans allowance are not young men. They are men of 50, some are getting close to 60 and others are also getting close to the time when they should receive old age pensions.
.
In view of the fact, as has already been pointed out, that many of these people are passing away, and passing away rapidly, the government should bring down legislation, if at all possible this session, and if not at this session at the beginning of the next session, to increase the war veterans allowances, as has been recommended by the Canadian Legion.
This matter was not lightly gone into by the Canadian Legion. They have looked into it very carefully, and I cannot see that in any way the requests of the government are unreasonable. The request of the Legion should be given most careful consideration and legislation along these lines should be brought down as soon as possible before any more of these burnt-out veterans pass away.

I have just a few words to say. We should give credit where credit is due. The government has done a fine job in helping the young men of the second world war. Many of us know young men who had not completed their education but who had hopes of doing so, and when the war broke out everything went by the board and they went overseas. The way in which these young men were sent back to school is an outstanding epic in the history of Canada. Some of them graduated in arts; some of them graduated in law and medicine. It is a credit to the government, but it is no more than the young men deserve.
I have had a little to do with the present Minister of Veterans Affairs. In the last ten years I have spent some weeks in Maniwaki, P.Q. There was a veteran there of the first war, an outstanding bushman who knew bush work, who was a specialist. When the second war broke out he was practically told by the enlisting officer that he was not doing his duty unless he used his gifts to head up men in the forestry battalion. He went. Eight years ago I advised him to get a pension. He was not fit to work. He could not hold his job. But there was a streak of independence in him which would not allow me to help him get his pension. Not six months ago he was unfit to work and was not able to take care of himself. I placed his case before the minister and he was received into hospital. He is now getting a pension which was his due. It is a credit to the minister.
I would like to add my tribute to the land settlement committee for the work it has done. I recommended a farm to the land settlement committee at Fort William. I took the man's word for it that it was fit to support a man, his wife and family. The committee then asked me to go out and see the farm for myself. There was a fine house on the farm, good stables, and some equipment, but it amounted to only 40 acres. That

farmer did not sell his farm to the credit of the land settlement committee. Of course, I lost a friend, or perhaps he was a friend. The land settlement committee has done a fine job and it is too bad it was not permitted to do the same kind of job after the second world war.
I heartily support the plea for an increase in the war veterans allowance. These men have given their best and they are not the men they were when they went overseas. They deserve the best this country can give. I also support the plea made on behalf of veterans who have reached the age of 60 and who served in a theatre of war; I do not think there should be a means test in their case when they reach the age of 60.
When I was home at Easter I spoke to a man who had four Christmas dinners in the trenches. You can visualize that man now with his feet all wet, sleeping in his clothes, with no comforts, and not knowing when he would be called across the river Jordan. I think we can rely on the Minister of Veterans Affairs to see to it that our veterans get a pension without a means test at the age of 60.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I do not see any reason why the veterans affairs committee should not be appointed permanently, because it is practically always the same members who serve on that committee. It is a very important committee and I just wish to say that I appreciate the services of the chairman. I also appreciate the services of the chairman of the pension board for the treatment given veterans at the lakehead-when I have presented cases for their consideration. I have failed in only one case, and cases are brought to my attention almost weekly.
I remember one case in particular-and I hope to revive it again-concerning a man who was in the first world war. One doctor, who was a specialist in his own line but who was not a soldiers' doctor, found he had shrapnel in his liver and being a Scotsman he went to work when he was not fit and finally had to be taken to the hospital. That man never got a pension and after a little while he passed on. In addition, his widow never received a pension and I hope some day that that woman will be treated as she ought to be.

Mr. Chairman, I am one of those who was very glad the government finally responded to the pleas of members of the house in regard to the setting up of a special committee on veterans affairs this year. Once again I wish to associate myself with other hon. members who not only this year but throughout the years have suggested that this committee should be a standing
Supply-Veterans Affairs committee of the house which could deal with the rapidly changing circumstances we meet from day to day which in turn call for a regular review of veterans legislation each year. Such a committee would give the veterans' organizations an opportunity to appear before it and bring to the attention of the committee the changes which may be necessary to make legislation more effective and serve veterans and their dependents to better advantage.
Before continuing I must say that the chairman of the committee in general did a good job indeed. All the members of the committee expressed that view before the committee concluded and I wish to say, in connection with the votes on the disputed amendment, that he is to be congratulated on doing his homework. I expressed my appreciation before and I might add here that he took a very long time to explain the reasons for his decision, he was very fair indeed in connection with the votes, records and conduct of the proceedings.
The committee did very good work on the four bills which were brought before it. I am not going to deal with them now at length. There were some very helpful amendments to the Canadian Pension Act, the War Service Grants Act, the Veterans Benefit Act. In dealing with these bills I know all the members of the committee appreciated the assistance given by the officials of the department.
I might add at this point that we are not criticizing the administration's officers. We are not criticizing their administration when dealing with the estimates. We are dealing with the question of legislation and criticizing the government on that score. In my opinion, and I think I am expressing the views of the members of the committee, the administration of our veterans legislation is in excellent hands so far as the officials are concerned and here I am referring to the Canadian pension commission and the war veterans allowance board and all the other administrative officers. I am sure the members of the committee appreciate the work they are doing to give effect to the will of parliament.
What we are trying to do this evening is to get the government to improve that legislation. As we have said before, we have excellent veterans legislation and I think without question it is the best in the world. But, as one hon. member said previously, that is not the sole standard. We should give what the Canadian nation can afford and within that amount do the best we can for veterans and their dependents. That is why we are urging certain amendments to the legislation this evening.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
Before leaving the question of the four bills dealt with in the committee I wish to support the suggestion made by the hon. member for Acadia with regard to an amendment to the Veterans Land Act. Generally speaking the amendments provided a great improvement in the act and will be of benefit to large numbers of veterans in Canada who have been unable to obtain satisfactory sites for home building under the present legislation. There are two points in particular on which I wish to support the hon. member. We are very sorry that the administration of a certain section of the act, after the preliminary work is done, is to come under Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Not that we are critical of that corporation, but the Veterans Land Act administration has a good record on behalf of veterans all across the country, and I am quite certain that the veterans of this country who are taking advantage of that act, or desire to take advantage of it, would prefer to come under the direct, efficient, and fair administration of the officials in charge of the Veterans Land Act administration.
I would like also to support the hon. member for Acadia with respect to his criticism of the increase in the interest rate. Now, the committee was helped a great deal by the representations made by the various national organizations, namely, the Canadian Legion, the British Empire Service League, the National Council of Veterans, the Canadian non-pensioned veterans widows and the Canadian merchant navy veterans association. Before passing on I want to say that I think it is only fair to express some admiration for the very valiant little body of widows who come to Ottawa once a year to present their views to the committee or, if the committee is not sitting, to the minister, his officials, or various members of parliament.
I shall always have the great distinction, Mr. Chairman, of having been the chairman of an unofficial veterans affairs committee called together by government and opposition members at which these ladies made their representations last session. I think at the time the minister was somewhat concerned about what was going on. One of the dear old ladies said to me, "What shall we do?" She said, "We want to have our say". Others said, "We have briefs". I said, "Do not turn up with a brief in your hands; keep it in your handbag. If Colonel Brooks asks if you have any representations to make, you can pull it out and make your representations". Everything went off very well indeed in that unofficial committee. I think these women
fMr. Herridge.]
all deserve a great deal of credit for having an interest in this question. I know they have been of assistance to the minister's officials on occasion because of their close association with veterans and their dependents in necessitous circumstances.
The Legion, as usual, made its excellent representation. I think all members of the committee would agree that the Legion has made a great contribution towards the development of veterans legislation in this country. I am sure that is a view that is accepted by all members of the committee. The record of the Legion proves that it has always had a sense of responsibility which included their responsibility to the veterans and their dependents in this country and as well their responsibility to the Canadian people, the taxpayers of Canada. On that account I think their representations are listened to with particular care. Whether people say so or not, they recognize that the Canadian Legion do not make representations to the cabinet, to the veterans affairs committee or to any other persons unless they are based on extremely strong grounds indeed. That is the foundation of the representations made to date.
The Legion came before this committee after making representations to the cabinet early in November. Certain officials of the Legion came before this committee and made further representations and they made an exceedingly helpful submission indeed. They dealt particularly with the necessity for an amendment to the War Veterans Allowance Act to increase the amount payable to single people to $60 a month and to married persons to $120 and to raise the permissive income.
I said that the Legion has a strong sense of responsibility. We all recognize that fact. They do not ask for something that the people of Canada cannot afford to pay or for something that is not badly needed. In addition to that consideration, the fact that their representations express the opinions of the rank and file and of many people in Canada is indicated by the resolutions that members of the House of Commons have received, not only from Legion branches- which is to be expected-and other veterans organizations but from women's organizations, from chambers of commerce and from other community organizations who recognize the need for some assistance to the veterans at this time, as well as letters from their own constituencies. I am sure every member of this committee has received a continuing correspondence which indicates the need for amendment of the legislation. The hon. member for Vancouver South, when speaking

this afternoon, indicated the need by mentioning certain facts. I think he mentioned the fact that one old veteran had committed suicide by gassing himself.
More than one.

More than one, the hon. member says. He also mentioned that their papers and correspondence indicated that the major cause of their trouble was economic, in that they could not exist on the present war veterans allowance.
Then there are the newspaper editorials. When you find large daily and weekly papers throughout Canada supporting the plea of the veterans, not on one occasion but repeatedly, there must be some extremely sound grounds for the representations of the Legion and for the representations that members of the house have made for amendment of the War Veterans Allowance Act. Newspapers try to reflect public opinion and, in order to maintain a certain popularity, to express in editorials and news items opinions that reflect what the people are thinking in the areas which they serve.
Before concluding I want to deal briefly with one editorial and to indicate the situation in British Columbia. I know that British Columbia is a bit of a thorn in the side of the minister and some members of the government with respect to veterans affairs but that is because the British Columbia people are the most progressive people in Canada. They are always looking ahead, and seeking improvements.
Modest people.

I must say, Mr. Chairman, that I was pleased to be associated with the hon. member for Royal in doing the things the people of Canada want us to do in this respect.
Here is an editorial from the Vancouver News-Herald of Wednesday morning, May 12. It is headed: " 'Burned Out' Veterans Living in Squalor; will Ottawa continue to be Callous?" Then we have another one here dated May 20-which shows that it is a current issue in British Columbia-which is headed: "In Their Time of Need, Ottawa Fails the Men who gave all but Life for Nation". Then there is another editorial of a subsequent date in similar vein. But I want to read this small news item which is headed: "Burned Out Vets Get Help Offers". I may say that this is from the News-Herald of May 20 of this year. It reads as follows:
The News-Herald is being flooded daily with calls from Vancouver citizens interested in the plight of "burned out" veterans, telling of tragic cases or offering help.
Supply-Veterans Affairs
The offers, from people in all walks of life, are only a drop in the bucket when one considers there are 10,000 men and women in Vancouver being forced to live on the $50 a month granted "Old Sweats" by the Veterans Allowance Act.
They cannot all be helped privately. Many will be forced to continue their pitiful existence: People like Fred B.
Fred is 61 and an accountant. Out of his $50 pension cheque he has 17 cents to keep him until the end of the month.
"I don't want charity from the government or anyone else," Fred maintains. "I want a job. Surely there is some place where my experience and ability would be valuable.
All the veterans allowance does for me is to keep me alive so that I can suffer the pangs of hunger over a long period and worry myself ill.
When the government can find time to discuss and endorse the raising of politicians' salaries,-"
I agree with that.
"-you'd think they could spare a little time to consider the plight of men and women in positions similar to my own.
When an election comes around we are the people. We are voters, 'loyal constituents,' the hand of friendship is held out. Once the owner of that hand is elected he proceeds to use it to pat his fellow party members on the back or to wave us aside as he says, 'Sorry, can't worry about you burned out bums this session.' "
We are extremely anxious to see something done about these unfortunate comrades this session. One could go on and read endlessly letters and news items that indicate the plight that many veterans and their dependents are suffering at the present time.
When we came to discuss this matter in the veterans affairs committee many of us realized that a unanimous resolution was adopted by the special parliamentary committee on veterans affairs in 1952 urging action on the war veterans allowance, that nothing was done to increase the over-all allowance for all who are entitled to receive war veterans allowance in Canada but only certain minor adjustments were made which were of benefit to the persons concerned. But even those adjustments are totally inadequate under present conditions. We felt that the Legion's representations to the committee-we had full knowledge of the situation as had all members of the House of Commons- further emphasized the need.
Because we know of the situation in the country, we felt that something should be done this session, and we felt that something should be done because the government has said "No". I do not believe in lying down when the government says "No". I believe that that is the time to start working all the harder. I am convinced that the work of the members of the House of Commons in connection with this legislation will finally produce results. Because the government said "No" to this crying need on the part of veterans and their dependents in Canada,

Supply-Veterans Affairs the hon. member for Royal moved his resolution urging that a recommendation be included in our report that the house extend the terms of reference of the veterans affairs committee-

That was not it at all. The hon. member wants to be correct on that point. That was the motion that the hon. member for Royal moved. The hon. member for Royal moved that the committee would go back to the house in order to have the terms of reference extended.
That is just what I am saying.
That is not what the hon. member said.
Oh, yes.
Pardon me; that is exactly what I said, namely that it be included in the report made to the house to ask the house to extend our terms of reference.
Exactly.

No, Mr. Chairman. Of course the chairman should be correct in this. There was already before the committee a report suggesting that very thing, namely, that the government give further consideration to the matter of the war veterans allowance and the merchant services. The motion of the hon. member for Royal had no reference at all to the report that the chairman had already read to the committee.
I want to correct the hon. member, Mr. Chairman-
I am correcting him now.
The hon. member needs to be corrected also, because there was no report before the committee at all.
The hon. member for Royal just made a political motion; that is all.

I object to that. The hon. member for Cape Breton South has supported these so-called political moves at every meeting of the veterans affairs committee. My motion was not political. As I pointed out there, if there was anything to be gained by playing politics the government would be the first to play politics and the first gainers would be the veterans. We had nothing to gain at all. The hon. member says that it was a political move, but may I say that time and time again since 1940 he has supported motions of the same kind in the veterans affairs committee. It is said that the hon. member is looking for a senatorship, and it has been noted that he has been showing more [Mr. Herridge.l
consideration for the government, especially in the veterans affairs committee, than he ever showed before.
The only suggestion I ever heard about a senatorship came from the communist press, and it would seem that my hon. friend is trying to help his own party by using their smear tactics in the house.
Anybody who says you are using smear tactics is using smear tactics himself.
I am more interested in getting something for the veteran.
You did not show it in the committee.
The motion of the hon. member for Royal was an impossibility and he knew it.
I did not know it.
I was interested in getting a report back to the house that said something about the matter rather than having six or seven opposition members vote for something that would have no effect whatsoever.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

Mr. Chairman, I was just dealing with the historic sequence of the motion moved by the hon. member for Royal prior to any report being made by the committee. I am not going to outline that any further.

Mr. Chairman, if the matter is in doubt I think that exactly what did happen should perhaps be put before the house. The draft report, which was drawn up by myself at the suggestion of several members of the committee, was before the committee and it was finally adopted in exactly the same form. It appears in volume No. 14 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the veterans affairs committee. The draft report was before the committee and it recited the fact that representations had been made urging changes in the War Veterans Allowance Act to raise the amount of allowance payable thereunder and also to raise the level of permissive income. We recommended that the government give sympathetic consideration to such submissions. To that there was an amendment moved that we ask for an extension of our terms of reference so that we could consider the War Veterans Allowance Act.
At this session.

The argument of the hon. member who has just spoken was to the

effect that even if we got the terms of reference extended we could not make a stronger recommendation than we were proposing to make and he suggested that if we endorsed the report unanimously it would be much better than passing a resolution to extend the terms of reference. That is exactly what the hon. member for Cape Breton South pointed out.
Did the hon. member who has just spoken say that my motion was an amendment to the report? It was not an amendment to the report at all. It was moved before the report was considered.
The draft report had been handed to the members of the committee.
The motion was made before that time.
Then the motion was made by the hon. member after that draft report was before the committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Kootenay West.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I thank the chairman of the special committee for the information he has given. That is exactly what I was explaining. I have a pretty good idea what happens in the committee and what goes on, and I am simply mentioning-
You were away for most of it.

Mr. Chairman, the hon.
member for Cape Breton South said that I was away for most of it.
That is right.

I am never away from the house or a committee unless I am ill or on some official duty. I was away from a few meetings on account of having to open an airport in my constituency, and I regretted having to be away at that time. Possibly the hon. member means on that account I overlooked some of the discussion.
That is right.

That may be right, but anyway my point is that the hon. member for Royal moved this motion and we saw fit to support it because it asked for action this session. I am not going into the question of the chairman's ruling or anything else, and I am not going to deal with that point further because what we are anxious to do is to get some action on the part of the government to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act. It is the sense of urgency and the need that caused members to urge action at this session.
Supply-Veterans Affairs
You do not get it by lying down to the government either.

No. The time is short. These old veterans are getting older and older. They are dropping off and many of them will not have the opportunity to receive the benefits of the legislative amendments that are required. That is why we fought for action at this session to increase the amount to $60 for a single veteran and $120 for a married veteran and to raise the permissive income, and we will continue to fight on behalf of our less fortunate comrades. This afternoon an hon. member suggested a figure of $3 million. I am not sure whether that is correct, but whether it is $3 million, $4 million or $15 million what a pitiful little sum it is out of our total production and wealth that is required to make happier the lives of these veterans and their dependents for whom we are fighting tonight and will continue to fight. They have not many more years to live, but I trust the government will take action soon so that many of them will enjoy the benefits of the legislation for which we are asking.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have been rather late in making remarks in the house but sometimes it is better to be late than a little too early. I am very happy that the first remarks I make rather extemporaneously should be with respect to the veterans of this country and in connection with a subject that is very close to our hearts. It has really done me a great deal of good to see how the house has considered these matters before it and the importance that various hon. members have placed on the subject that we are discussing.
In listening to the hon. members who have spoken one point comes to my mind that I do not think has been raised and it has to do with veterans pensions and allowances as they concern dependent parents. We have been speaking of the pensioners themselves and of their widows, and I should like to say a few words about dependent parents. What I am going to say arises out of my own experience with two cases that have come to my attention within the last few months. Not long ago a mother came to me whose son had been killed in the first world war. Over the years she has been receiving a pension of $40 a month on behalf of her deceased son. She became eligible for the old age pension and received the pension. In due course she was notified that she would no longer be eligible for the pension awarded her under the veterans legislation. That was a very great hardship because I think the understanding is that the old age pension

Supply-Veterans Affairs comes as something extra, something to help men and women to have a little extra in life.
The effect of not raising the exemption for veterans and the allowances they are permitted to have before the pension is taken away from them is really to penalize the veterans, and I think we are also penalizing the parents because we are making it a penalty to receive the old age pension.
It is fundamental that the minister and the government should consider this question and place it in its proper perspective. I believe the parents of sons who have gone overseas, and who have not returned, people who have given everything they have to this country, are still entitled to receive the reimbursement for the actions of their sons and daughters, and at the same time should be entitled to the pension every other man and place it in its proper prospective. I country receives. On behalf of these parents I ask that this matter be given consideration by the minister and by this government.

I do not intend to take up very much of the time of the committee this evening, but there is one point I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. It concerns the bachelor who has earned rehabilitation credits, but because of the regulation controlling these rehabilitation credits finds it impossible to draw them. If a person has no dependents, it is not much satisfaction for him to take out insurance that can be paid only at his death or at a time when he is so old it is not of much value. If he is living in a boarding house there is nothing that he can buy for which he could use his re-establishment credit. If he is not working at a job where he requires an automobile or some other equipment necessary for the job, he cannot spend the credit on that.
There must be some people who are in a position where they cannot draw their reestablishment credits. I would think that at this time it would be proper, when most of the veterans have re-established themselves, that those who have not used their re-establishment credits and who cannot draw them by reason of the regulations, should be permitted to use those credits to purchase a 20-year endowment insurance policy. A change could be made in the regulations to permit the veteran to do this. Then, he would have this money, along with some more he might have added to it, upon which to draw. I would sincerely recommend to the minister that for the sake of the veterans who are entitled to re-establishment credits, and who have been unable to draw them, a change should be made in the regulations.

I was pleased to see that the Department of Veterans Affairs saw fit to change so many of the acts applying to veterans at this session. This gave veterans an opportunity to take advantage of the improvements in these acts. I am pleased also to see that we have such a stalwart in the person of the hon. member for Fort William, who is so interested in helping people. I believe we could all say it does not matter who it is; he is always ready to assist the war veterans or anyone else out of his great generosity. I should like to say that I hope the government itself will endorse some of the things he advocates, and that he can get a little closer to the heart of the government so that we can get a little more for these war veterans who are on allowances. For a few moments I was afraid we were going to hear the truth about the truth about the truth about the War Veterans Allowance Act, similar to what we heard in connection with the wheat situation a few days ago. However, we finally got that straightened out, and the facts were put properly by the chairman of the committee.
I am not a member of the veterans affairs committee, and therefore have a possibly somewhat different point of view in connection with this War Veterans Allowance Act. I am the representative of the New Westminster riding which probably, on a per capita basis, has a greater number of recipients of war veterans allowance than any other riding in the dominion. There are approximately 9,200 war veterans in the province of British Columbia who come under that act. I would say that represents about a quarter of the total in all of Canada. Because of the fact we have a fine climate and everything that goes with it on the lower mainland, most of them apparently have settled in my particular riding. The hon. member for Fraser Valley says the same is true of his riding.
Possibly I should take a moment or two to draw your attention to the history of this particular subject, but I do not believe it is necessary. All of us are familiar with how the resolution was introduced, how everyone tried to take part in the debate and how we were stopped; how the terms of reference were limited and the matter was referred to the committee for study. We were all very frustrated by the thought we were not going to be able to do anything for the war veterans before the estimates came down, and such proved to be the case.
Then some hon. members, including myself, gave notice of a resolution asking that this question of the burnt-out pensioners be raised. The purpose behind such

a resolution-I am not going to discuss it at any length-was to draw the attention of the government to this problem in the hope that if they did not do something this year they would do something next year. I will not be like the hon. member for Assiniboia and sit down, but if the government will promise to do something about the matter I shall remove my resolution from the order paper tomorrow.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, presented a resolution along similar lines to the veterans affairs committee. I would have you note that they are members of the party that is in power. I might say there were literally dozens of people in this house who, during the throne speech debate, indicated the desirability of increasing the war veterans allowance. Now, because of the fact that the terms of reference to the veterans affairs committee were so limited, there was a great deal of disappointment expressed amongst three groups of people particularly; members of parliament, the war veterans themselves, and the people of Canada as a whole. The members of parliament were somewhat disappointed because every party in this house has indicated from time to time that they wanted an increase in that allowance. The veterans themselves felt that they were not "off the beam", and that they were not asking too much in their brief.
The fact is that they had been assured during the recent election campaign that everything would be done to institute these particular claims. Many of the claims were endorsed by members of the Liberal party in British Columbia. I must say that those gentlemen had the decency to stand up and reiterate those requests. The people of Canada do feel quite badly about this. They feel, and I would number myself amongst the group, that we have broken faith to a large degree with the war veterans. We have promised them something in the way of assistance for the past two years, and they are still looking for it.
This government has been frank in telling the veterans when they first came there would be nothing for them. As a result of that each one of us was deluged with a large number of letters asking that we entreat the government to take another look. I am sure the Prime Minister and the Minister of Veterans Affairs received the same letters and telegrams, or copies of them, that were received in my office. And still the answer was, no. Some of the letters read: We do not have enough food. Or they might read: We have enough food and enough money for 83276-391i
Supply-Veterans Affairs taxes and utilities, but we have nothing left to buy clothing. The story is a difficult one, and I received telegrams from every branch of the Legion in my riding-and there are 8 of them. I am sure every branch in Canada must have sent telegrams to the minister asking him to help them get this allowance.
Why did not the minister entertain the question, or take another look at it? Was it a question as to whether the government could afford to spend $3 million? Well, the answer is this: Can we afford democracy? In many instances these men, while they did not give their lives, most certainly were willing to do so if need be. Yet, at their request, apparently we are not willing to give them a decent living.
I do not want to go into the gruesome details about suicide, and the like, which have been mentioned. But that is some indication of the need. The question could be asked: What can we give? There, again, they were willing to give their lives. What prayers did the people of this country offer when the Germans were standing at the gates of Paris? The people were ready to give practically anything so long as the boys would stand there and either hold the line or push the enemy back. Those men were not found wanting; but apparently now we, as a parliament, are found wanting. Perhaps I should not say "parliament"; I should say the government. I know parliament would endorse this plea if hon. members were given the privilege to vote upon it.
In connection with the problem one must keep in mind that there are several different types of veterans, each of which must be dealt with on his own merits. I should like to read to the committee two brief articles appearing in issues of Corps-Vet, a magazine published in New Westminster. I suggest these articles will indicate to some degree the nature of the problem in my riding. I know the minister is familiar with some of the facts, but I do not think he knows all of them. There is one of which I would ask him to take particular notice-because we have many grave problems there. The article to which I shall refer first is written by J. H. Thompson, who is secretary-manager of the New Westminster Legion. If I were to give him a title I would call him Mr. Canadian Legion. This article is headed "Jungle Town", and states:
As we go to press the population of our little known "Jungle Town" thrives with activity-or perhaps I should say, inactivity. The inhabitants are a motley bunch-human flotsam-who at the first hint of winter's snow hit the road for the Pacific coast. Here, along the dikes of the Fraser river, they share their frugal and miserable existence with the old-timers who have been established for many years in the area. They are the personification of the seedy side of our enlightened race.

Supply-Veterans Affairs < * Some are alcoholics who, in a few short years, become winos and rubby-dubs-the drinkers of extract and shaving lotion. Others are ex-convicts, petty thieves or just plain deadbeats-while a small minority are simply broke with no place to turn fdr assistance. From November to March they 3Jve in near animal fashion in shanties built from tar paper and box wood-many without the luxury of a floor while the river provides their plumbing and fuel supply.
. Through necessity they share their worldly wealth -which is food and wine. Forage parties are on the prowl every day-some depend on the more simple and direct method of begging coins from citizens on the street-others line up at the welfare agencies for a small grocery order. If the "loot" for the day is good, some of the groceries are converted to cash for the purchase of wine and extracts and the celebration is on. A few days Jater they emerge from the shacks weak and exhausted-sick in body and mind-then the cycle starts all over.
You might well ask-"Who are these characters? Where do they come from? Have they always been misfits in our way of life? and What are the authorities doing about it?"
Each and every one has a story to tell-sordid- but human nevertheless. Many came from good homes-others from the tenement and skidrow districts of our Canadian cities. To the vast majority $he key that opened this depraved life for them was alcohol-and yet we know that each and every one of these derelicts who allowed alcohol to ruin ilieir lives, did so for a reason. We do know that close to forty per cent of Jungle Towners are veterans. A few years ago the veterans from world war II in this category were exceptional, now they outnumber the old diehards.
' This problem is, and will remain, a challenge, npt only to the authorities but to the legion. After two world wars we realize only too well how messy wars can get-and it's not all on the battlefield. ISTb two humans will react to warfare in a like manner-some can go through it and become readjusted to normal peacetime living without any trouble-others may take years to become rehabilitated.
I shall not read further, but I believe placing this article on the record has served a, useful purpose. Some years ago veterans of world war II were the exception in Jungle Town, whereas today 40 per cent of them are veterans. Certainly they are there in greater numbers than the diehards. This Article appeared in the issue of February, 1954. Then I would quote the following article from the issue of June, 1954. It is headed "Too Little", and states:
Charlie had served his country well-perhaps too well-for in so doing the effect of battle fatigue through two major wars had taken its toll . . . Charlie and his wife found they were obliged to exist and raise their young family of four youngsters on the war veterans allowance.
In desperation, like many more in this low income group, they moved their few worldly possessions from the city to a small acreage in the country where land was cheap and taxes low . . . and where a small garden and a few chickens can do wonders to fill the tummies of four growing youngsters. With the small nest egg he had somehow managed to set aside, a small two room shack was laboriously erected. Charlie was no carpenter
'Mr. Hahn.]
and his health was rapidly becoming a problem. However, necessity won out and at last they had a roof over their heads.
From this humble beginning they planned and tried to save every odd penny to enlarge their home-sleeping six in a small bedroom left much to be desired. Finally by scrounging and more sacrifice the long planned-for addition was started and the frame work erected and then fate once again stepped into the picture.
I should add that this man was one of the war veterans who would be entitled to an increase in the war veterans allowance. He went on to try to complete the building of this shack, but failed. He could not do it himself. It was a case of the Legion stepping in to help. The article goes on to say:
As we go to press the job of rebuilding their home is completed but for many months-perhaps years-our service bureau will be giving this family a friendly and helping hand . . .Charlie has finally answered the last roll call and passed on to a more pleasant and peaceful life.
This man tried to help himself. He is the fellow we should be interested in, and we should be interested in him right in this parliament; to assist him in every way, shape and form to become a citizen who wants to continue to feel that Canada has not let him down.
These men could not come to Ottawa. They sent their emissary, and the emissary has had to go back and say, "The job was not accomplished. It was not completed, so far as war veterans allowances are concerned." That is the part that those veterans are particularly interested in.
