I would tell this government, Which has been so often aptly likened to the ostrich, which has so large a body and has so little sight, that it has denied us the privilege of discussing this vital question until the dying days of this session. We are justified in saying that this question should have been brought to the attention of the house when we asked for it, and it should have been discussed earlier.
So far as the increase itself is concerned, it may be argued from time to time that it is supposed to be equivalent to the old age pension, it is supposed to take its place. I point out to the minister that in Alberta and in British Columbia today the old age pensioner, if he is that destitute, is entitled to $40 plus $15 a month, or $55 a month, which is more than we are giving to our war veterans, the men who helped to defend our country.
In connection with these other items, I heartily endorse the idea that the permissive income should be increased. I do not understand just exactly why there is a ceiling on the permissive income. It may be possible to explain it, and I should like to hear the

explanation. I shall be glad to listen to it. It should be increased from what it is today to $1,200 for a single man and $2,000 for a married man, which is barely sufficient to keep body and soul together when one can receive such a low permissive income.
One other question has been raised, namely, the eligibility of the imperial war veteran who has married a Canadian. I have a case in mind of an imperial war veteran who married a Newfoundland girl quite a number of years ago following the first war. This particular man has lived on and off in Canada and in Newfoundland. He has also been in the United States, but he has not been here for the full 20-year period and therefore he is not eligible, even though his wife is a Canadian by birth. I do not think that that is quite playing the game. The reason for the man to come to Canada originally was that he wanted to be a Canadian. I think the 20-year period is too long. Other instances were pointed out earlier. A widow does not become eligible because her husband may have died before he had put in the 20-year period, and therefore she never becomes eligible even though she may be a Canadian by birth.
In conclusion I should like to summarize my suggestions as follows:	First, increase
the allowance as requested by the Legion to $60 and $120 respectively, second the permissive ceiling should be increased; third, make the Canadian imperial war veterans of world war I eligible for the burnt-out pension and the allowance before they have resided here 20 years; I would say that possibly 10 years is sufficient; fourth, a permanent committee on veterans affairs should be set up.
I see no reason for not setting up a permanent committee on veterans affairs. I do not believe anyone does. This problem has to do with war veterans allowances. Those are not all the veterans problems we are going to have. There are many committees that we name each year that never meet. If we do not need to meet we will not meet. Certainly we should have a standing committee on veterans affairs.
My fifth suggestion is that this government take notice now of this problem and at the earliest possible date implement the increase in the allowances along the lines of the war veterans request. My final suggestion is that in future the committee be not hamstrung in its terms of reference because if it is set up for the purpose of discussing veterans affairs or any other affairs, let it discuss all of them.

I do not want to let this opporr tunity pass, even at the risk of prolonging the debate a little, without paying tribute to those who were responsible and still are responsible for the administration of the Veterans Land Act. I had the pleasure of sitting on the veterans committee. It was my first committee, and I must say that I found it a most valuable experience. I think members of that committee were unanimous in their endorsation of the brief we had presented to us by the director of the Veterans Land Act, Brigadier Rutherford.
I would like to spend a few moments discussing that briefly. I am particularly interested in this because in my riding I have some 1,124 different small holders units constructed under this act, and it is a very vital part of York-Scarborough. There must have been some moments of anxiety when the Veterans Land Act was first introduced. It was said primarily to be a scheme to settle the veterans on the land, I think probably with tongue in cheek. Everyone knew that it also was a housing program, particularly in the metropolitan areas. In some cases, and perhaps in most, that is what it has really developed into. Of course problems arise in that connection when you get away from the original principle of ah act. However, the act has been a tremendous success. We know that as of December 31, 1953 some 63,000 veterans were settled on holdings, either as full-time farmers or on small holdings in Canada.
The soundness of the scheme depended on two things. First, you had to have a well drawn and executed act, well administered; and, as I said, we have had unanimous endorsation in that regard. On the other hand, the other factor has been the veteran himself. In this regard we have found our veterans to be most industrious, most capable and most ingenious in utilizing the benefits given to them under this act. They literally carved themselves a home out of the wilderness in some cases. As I say, under the benefits of this act the veterans have really come through in a grand way, and I am happy to see that we are extending the benefits of the act. I hope we shall see many more veterans take advantage of the extended provision that we are providing under the new amended bill.
The figures in connection with the settler ments under the act do make wonderful reading. We find that of the 63,000 who were settled under the act, only 114 have been put off owing to non-compliance with their original contract. Of 26,500 small holders, as of April 30, 1954, only 44 of them were in any

Supply-Veterans Affairs way in arrears on their payments. I really do admire the veterans for the way they have carried out their part of the agreement. Only 44 out of 26,000, that is fewer than 2 per thousand, had in any way fallen into arrears in regard to the small holdings and payments on their mortgages.
As I say, in my riding I have 1,124 of these; in Willowdale, about 433, in Agincourt and Scarborough, about 372; and in Highland Creek 319. I have been out to these holdings several times, particularly in the Homeland subdivision in Scarborough, and hon. members would be very proud of the way these veterans have kept and developed their homes. They are men who work during the day. In some cases they have 2 acres, and in many cases one-half an acre; in any event, a large area of land. They have planted grass seed; they have developed gardens and they have really turned those areas into beauty spots. They deserve a great deal of credit. This is reflected in the increased value of the land. When the land was purchased the original cost was about $300 million. That was the estimated cost of the actual land when it was first purchased all across Canada, but the present estimate of the appraisers in the department is something more than $500 million. This, of course, is due to improvements made by the veterans and the natural increase in the value of land around metropolitan areas.
This brings up the problem that one finds in metropolitan areas. When you have land appreciating in value the interest and taxes on that land, or the municipal assessment increases, and in some cases the veterans have found it, I would not say hard but they have complained about the increase in municipal taxes on large holdings such as they have. However, I was pleased to note that during the last session the Ontario legislature amended the Ontario municipal act wherein it was provided that any municipality may pass a bylaw giving special consideration to veterans settled on these subdivisions in regard to municipal assessments and taxes. In that connection the townships of Scarborough and North York and in fact most other municipalities in metropolitan Toronto have taken action and the veterans find themselves assessed on something that is more like a rural assessment basis than the usual metropolitan rates, so that the problem has been partially overcome.
But the veterans, I understand, have been very fortunate in most cases around Toronto because the land values have increased so markedly that it has been possible for veterans to sell their complete holding and obtain enough money to help them out of their total


indebtedness under the act. He can sell part of the holding if he does not require it, and that has been done. As a matter of fact, if this is done before the ten years expires under his contract the veteran finds in many cases that he gets such a good price for the land that he can cheerfully forgo the $1,400 additional grant to which he is entitled if he carries out the contract in full.
However, the surprising thing is that even under such circumstances, when the land is so valuable, the veteran has not been subdividing the land. That has been my experience. They are accustomed to living in these spacious and beautiful surroundings on which they have worked so hard, and it would be difficult, although the value of the land has skyrocketed, for them to give up this land even though by the sale of it they would be in an extremely good financial position. I think that shows a very good attitude on the part of the veterans.
As we all know, part II of the act now allows veterans to obtain assistance in building their own homes with a 10 per cent down payment either in cash or kind and the maximum amount of the loan under the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is $8,000. I believe we will find a great many veterans taking advantage of this section of the act. There are many veterans who find themselves saddled with an expensive home and they will be able to sell that home and build their own home under part II of the act as long as it is approved by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. They can take the equity out of the home they sell and put their own, shall we say, sweat, into building a home of their own and save $2,000, perhaps more, and so put themselves on a sound financial basis. I know that many veterans in Toronto have been looking forward to a scheme such as this. The important part of this scheme is the supervision and assistance they will receive in acting as their own contractors. This has proved very successful under the act so far. We have about 6,000 homes in Canada built entirely by veterans acting as their own contractors, and about 1,700 to 2,000 are under way at the present time.
I think we can depend on the veterans to make the new part II of the act work just as well as they made the old provision work under the old act, and I look forward to very many years of pleasant association with veterans in my own riding under this scheme. I want to pay tribute to Mr. Rutherford and his office staff for the manner in which they have carried out the provisions of the act. They have helped in no small measure to make it work successfully and I know they will carry on doing so.

Mr. Chairman, the veterans affairs committee at this session did, I think we will all agree, a very good job on the bills which were submitted to it. I am not going to take up the time of the committee to go into what was done in regard to these bills, including the Veterans Land Act, except to say that we received an extremely good briefing in regard to the matter and an extremely good picture of what was done under the Veterans Land Act and what the officials hoped will be done in future.
As a result of the evidence made available to us by the various veterans organizations and by way of consultation with the members, I think we succeeded in dealing with the bills effectively. Amendments were made, I think, to all the bills which were presented to us and in fact there were quite a number of amendments to some of them. I think as a result of these amendments the legislation was considerably improved.
There were, however, a few deficiencies in the amendments to the Veterans Land Act which I am sorry to see the government did not correct. I agree with other hon. members who have already pointed out that the rate of interest should have been lowered and could have been made the same as on the small holdings and farms secured under the Veterans Land Act. I think the down payment for houses should be considerably lower in some cases. Under the present provision there is an inflexible down payment provision. I do not see any reason whatever to insist on that provision. The thing could have been made flexible to enable those veterans who wanted to build a home under the act to do so. If there had been a flexible down payment many more could have taken advantage of the act.
Now, the outstanding thing as far as veterans affairs are concerned this year, and the one thing above all others of interest to veterans, and on which they want something done, is a matter which we were not allowed to discuss and on which we were not allowed to make recommendations in committee. That is the matter of war veterans allowances. I think there is no question about the fact that the rate of the war veterans allowance should be increased and the amount of allowable income should be increased. That has been dealt with by a number of people and I am not going to go into the various reasons which could be advanced as to why this improvement is imperative. I would say that a large number of veterans receiving the war veterans allowance are not receiving enough to support themselves and they are having an extraordinarily difficult time. In
Supply-Veterans Affairs many cases they are unable to get enough to eat after they have paid their rent and so forth. This is undoubtedly a situation which should not have been allowed to continue, though it appears the government is quite prepared to allow it to continue beyond this session.
The position in Alberta and British Columbia has already been mentioned. The amount of war veterans allowance vis-a-vis the old age pension is such that you have a situation, I am told, where a German soldier who fought against our troops in the first war is receiving more money under old age pension than the Canadian soldier who fought against him. I am told that in one case that situation actually exists, and it is a situation which can exist so far as quite a considerable number of people are concerned. Despite that the government has taken no action to correct the situation. Anyone who comes to this country and lives here for 20 years and reaches the age of 70, no matter from where he comes, qualifies as a citizen, and such a man is now in a better position in Alberta and British Columbia than is the veteran of the first war who, as I say, may have fought against those people in that war. This is a situation which naturally causes bitterness. How can you expect the people who fought for this country in the first war, when they hear of a situation such as this, to be anything but bitter about it, particularly when they themselves are, as I say, in some cases not receiving enough income to be able to get enough to eat, really.
During this debate the members of this party have been accused of playing politics in the matter of the war veterans allowance. I take grave exception to that accusation, whether it has been made directly, as I think it was in one case, or whether it has been put out by inference. The people who are playing politics in this matter are the people on the government side of the house. They are the people who are trying to play politics with regard to the matter. As a matter of fact, these members are saying that this thing must be corrected, that they would like to see the war veterans allowance increased and that they would like to see the allowable earnings increased and so forth but that there is nothing they can do about it as the government says "No."
As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, some of the speeches I have heard in connection with this matter here in this chamber and in the committee appeared to me to be nothing else but sickening hypocrisy. I feel strongly on this matter. When people come out and say:	Oh, yes; I am entirely in

Supply-Veterans Affairs favour of increasing the war veterans allowance; I am entirely in favour of the Legion brief and so forth, and then demonstrate that belief by voting against every possible motion which would cause it to be implemented, then, as I say, it just does not add up.
The hon. member for Vancouver South, in speaking this afternoon, said he was delighted that the first speech he made in the house was in favour of the war veterans allowance and that this, which would be his last speech, was on the same subject, and that he gave his unqualified support to the Legion brief with regard to an increase in the war veterans allowance. He demonstrated his unqualified support of the Legion brief by voting against every motion in the House of Commons and every motion in the committee which could have implemented that Legion brief. That was how he demonstrated his unqualified support for this increase.

The record of the committee is there. I will leave the matter to the judgment of the veterans of this country. In his speech this afternoon the hon. member said the government was not able to increase the war veterans allowance this year. He says they are not able to do it. My goodness, Mr. Chairman, what does he mean by saying that they are not able to do it? There is no question at all of ability to do it. It is a matter of refusal to do it. Any statement along that line indicates, as a matter of fact, the true interest of the hon. member in the

welfare of the veterans allowance recipients and the desire which the hon. member has to have this allowance increased. He says the government was not able to do it. As was pointed out previously, it would mean a mere matter of a few million dollars. Yet he says the government is not able to do it! The government refuses to do it; the government will not do it, and that is the only reason it is not done. No question whatever of ability to do it is involved in the matter.
I must say that I was also disappointed in the hon. member for Cape Breton South this afternoon.
That is going to hurt his feelings.

The hon. member for Cape Breton South said he had voted against this motion made in the committee by the hon. member for Royal because of a former vote in the house and because the Prime Minister said that nothing would be done this year about the war veterans allowance. He said that in the committee and he said it again today. For a man who used to be such a bonny fighter as was the hon. member for Cape Breton South to say that he could not support this motion-which really meant an increase in the war veterans allowance- because the Prime Minister, forsooth, had said he did not want it this session, is difficult for me to understand.
Mr. Chairman-
The hon. member for Cape Breton South has certainly changed.
Wrong again!
On what sort of question is the hon. member up on his feet? Is this a point of order, a question of privilege or just a speech?
I am just going to ask the hon. member a question.
That is fine.

This is one hon. member who I think is inclined to be fair. I should like to ask him if he has read the record. If he has read the record he will know that the motion was on a ruling of the chairman and that it had nothing at all to do with the subject he is talking about.

The hon. member knows that there is no use asking me if I read the record. He knows that I was there every minute during which this discussion went on. I know the whole discussion. I heard the whole thing and so on. What the hon. member is doing is quibbling over a technicality. That is what he is doing. He knows
Supply-Veterans Affairs as well as does every other member of that committee that the vote essentially was an effort-the last one we could make-to try to get the war veterans allowance increased at this session. As a matter of fact, because the Prime Minister said there would be no action on it this year, the member said: "Oh well, I will vote against it". This is not typical of the hon. member as I have known him in the nine years that I have been a member of the house.
What reason would there be for that?

I am not imputing any reasons or motives at all. I merely say that I am disappointed. I was disappointed that the hon. member should express the views he did in that regard and then turn around this afternoon and accuse the hon. member for Royal of playing politics with this matter.
That is right.
Hear, hear.
The thing is completely ridiculous.

Royal always does play
politics.

I am glad to say that the hon. member for Cape Breton South did not take this defeatist attitude in 1948. As a matter of fact, the prime minister of that time, Mr. Mackenzie King, announced in the house in 1947, to begin with, after a great deal of pressure had been put upon him to take action, that pensions would be increased 10 per cent and that was all. Then we went home for Christmas. There was a great deal of agitation and many representations made, and when we came back after Christmas the prime minister had weakened and he got up and said that he had reconsidered the matter and that the pensions would be increased 15 per cent but that that was the absolute limit. Standing right there he said that under no circumstances would they be increased more than 15 per cent. Did the hon. member for Cape Breton South take a defeatist attitude? Did the rest of us take that attitude? No, Mr. Chairman. When the committee met we went to work on this thing and insisted-
Mr. Chairman-
Order.
The hon. member asked me a question.
No, I did not ask him a question. If the hon. member wants to ask a question he can do so in a minute. I want to finish what I am saying.

Sit down.
