speechtext: Order. Will the hon. member for Calgary North also take his seat. May I remind hon. members that the hon. member who has the floor cannot be interrupted without his consent.
Hear, hear.
That is a better ruling.

As I was saying, the prime minister said that 15 per cent was the absolute maximum. The members of the veterans affairs committee did not accept that as final. They did not say: Well, the prime minister said that is final and we cannot go any further. We pounded and pounded away at the matter.
You did not force any votes in the house on it.

As a matter of fact we moved motions in the committee. The hon. member for Royal moved that the pension should be increased by 33J per cent, and that is what the veterans are receiving now. At that time that motion was defeated but a motion that they should be increased by 25 per cent was passed unanimously by the committee. The matter came back to the house and that recommendation was adopted. Instead of what the prime minister had said the pension was increased by 25 per cent. If we had had the defeatist attitude at that time that the hon. member for Cape Breton South has shown on this occasion the veterans would have had an increase of 15 per cent in their pensions instead of the 25 per cent which they got and the 33J per cent which they have at the present time. The only way you can get things is to fight for them. As far as I am concerned I am going to continue to fight for an increase in the war veterans allowance and in the ceilings and I am not going to be deterred by what the Prime Minister or anybody else says.
Have your own way.

As a matter of fact, unless the government comes around to making this change in the fairly near future they are going to have a much greater storm on their heads from the veterans of this country than already exists.

Mr. Chairman, I will not take very long. I do not think I can clear up the misconception that seems to be abroad about the particular vote that was taken in the committee, but I should like to express my point of view. To me it was not a vote on

the merits or demerits of the veterans allowance act at all. If it had been I believe that every member of that committee would have been in favour of taking some action about the war veterans allowance. It was a vote to sustain the chairman's ruling, the chairman having ruled that we did not have the power to deal with a subject that was beyond our terms of reference. I listened very carefully. I think the chairman took about an hour and a half to quote citations and to explain similar situations that had happened in the past. I also listened to the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and others who expressed different views. After listening carefully I came to my own personal conclusion that the chairman was correct, and for that reason I supported him. But I supported him on that point only. If the War Veterans Allowance Act had been at stake I would not have supported him. I supported him because I considered, excellent chairman that he was, that he had given a true and faithful interpretation of all the authorities he quoted.
But I felt then and still do that the minister and the government were remiss in their duty in not referring the War Veterans Allowance Act for the consideration of the committee. On behalf of the veterans of my constituency I must register a protest and express their great disappointment that this subject was excluded from the consideration of the committee. The plight of veterans widows should also have been referred to the committee for attention. I fail to understand why the minister did not include these matters in the terms of reference. The minister has been questioned about these matters but so far he has refused to commit himself one way or the other. Before the session is over I think he should definitely say what he intends to do for the war veterans of Canada so that the Legion and others who are anxious to have something tangible done soon will know where they stand.
I am sure that the minister must be aware of the distress and dissatisfaction of the veterans and their widows. The average member of the house receives many letters and telegrams on the subject. Therefore it is quite safe to assume that the minister would receive a great deal more and should be thoroughly conversant with the difficulties faced by the war veterans and widows who are forced to live on a substandard diet in a country as rich and prosperous as we claim ours is. It puzzles me why the minister, being aware of their plight, ignored the whole problem when setting up the terms of reference of the committee.

It cannot be said that we cannot afford the cost. Another member referred to that. It cannot be said that the burden is already too great because I would point out that the total cost of administering the veterans affairs department, providing for all pensions, disability pensions, widows pensions, war veterans allowances, providing for the upkeep and administration of the various hospitals and other buildings, the administration of the pension commission, welfare services, soldier settlement services, the Veterans Land Act, rehabilitation benefits, re-establishment credits and numerous other items, including the minister's own salary, only amounts to a slight fraction over 5 per cent of the federal budget this year.
To my mind that is a very small price to pay to look after Canadian veterans of three wars whose sacrifices have made it possible for us to enjoy our lives and possessions in peace. In spite of the increased cost of living and the greater need of these veterans, particularly the burnt-out pensioners about whom we have been talking, the department has actually reduced its estimated requirements for the current year. I cannot understand that. The government is in the happy position, with an expanding economy and surpluses, of being able to share our wealth with other less fortunate nations, some of whom were our enemies not long ago. I do not criticize them for that. I think we are doing a kindly act, but surely if we can do that Canada's defenders deserve more than a brush-off when they ask to have their problems reviewed by the special committee on veterans affairs.
The previous committee was unanimous in recommending that something should be done for veterans allowance recipients. The members of this committee, too, I believe were unanimous in their sympathy for the recipients of war veterans allowances, but their hands were tied by the government. I am not blaming the chairman of the committee. I believe if he had had it in his power he would have extended the powers of the committee. I submit that the minister and the government deliberately tied the hands of the committee so that they could not deal with this subject.
The chairman of the committee did include in the report a request for sympathetic consideration of war veterans and the merchant marine. Possibly he was exceeding the terms of reference by going even that far, I cannot say. But I sincerely hope that the minister will pay attention to that recommendation, as well as to the numerous briefs presented to the committee on the subject by the various organizations.
Supply-Veterans Affairs
In my opinion the work done by the committee was excellent as far as it went. Several desirable changes were made in the bills before us, and accepted by the government. This proved one thing conclusively to me, and that was that the good work done by this committee should be continued by the formation of a standing committee. I am sure the minister would gain valuable assistance in the administration of this department, and definitely the veterans would secure valuable aid in solving their numerous problems. I wholeheartedly support the Canadian Legion brief. These people have done an excellent piece of work in presenting it, and trying to solve the problems in the way they have recommended.
I should like also to draw one other thing to the minister's attention. This matter cannot wait for attention by the standing committee, but is urgent and touches on the plight of the widows of veterans who die while in receipt of a pension for less than a 50 per cent disability. I have a letter here from the British Columbia branch of the Canadian Legion drawing attention to the widows' position. I should like to quote it.
We would point out that, as the whole intent of the Pension Act is to provide benefits strictly in accord with the degree of war disability, it would seem quite evident that at present most of the trouble as far as the widow is concerned, lies in the fact that there is too great a difference between the benefits provided for a 50 per cent and a 45 per cent disability.
A person with a 50 per cent disability gets a 30 per cent increase between the ages of 55 and 59 years; but a 45 per cent pension gets no increase. This ultimately hurts the widow when, on the death of the veteran, the pension is under 50 per cent. It is extremely hard to believe that if a 50 per cent disability can prove so burdensome with advancing years as to warrant three successive 10 per cent increases, a 45 per cent fixed assessment is entirely unaffected by age and so warrants no increase.
It should be pointed out that where a widow is left when the pension is at 50 per cent, she receives $100 per month; but the widow of a pensioner who dies with less than a 50 per cent disability pension, say 48 per cent or 49 per cent, gets nothing at all. Where children are left under similar circumstances, the children of the veteran on a 50 per cent disability pension get pensions at the orphan rate, which is double the 100 per cent rate, but the children of a veteran on a 45 per cent disability pension receive nothing.
With all due respect to the minister, I believe he should pay urgent and special attention to these widows, who are numerous. I am sorry they are numerous. They are

Supply-Veterans Affairs numerous because of the hard classification that the pensioner has to undergo to get a pension at all. Possibly there are far too many veterans who get less than 50 per cent, and so far as the widows are concerned more generous treatment should be accorded to them. I hope that the minister will take that under advisement.

In listening to the discussion of this item today and the debates that have taken place earlier in this session on the question of veterans, I believe two points stand out and should be emphasized. The first of these is the success that has been achieved by the special committee on veterans affairs, not only this year but in previous years. The success has been achieved in spite of a certain amount of internal wrangling in which there has been a difference of opinion as to the best approach to achieve the one aim of every member of that committee, namely, the improvement of the position of the veterans. I honestly believe that considerable progress has been made by these veterans affairs committees over the period of many years. I sincerely hope that they will continue, and if there is a certain amount of internecine strife it is only because various members of that committee are so anxious to achieve something for the veterans that they believe the means they are advocating are the best way in which to achieve those ends. When you get people really worked up in their effort to try to do something for the cause, it is inevitable that there is a certain amount of heat engendered, but that is very largely on the surface. There is a genuine effort by all members of the committee to achieve a great end.
The second point that I think should be underlined is the fact that the committee this year was rather restricted in its terms of reference and therefore was not able to examine as many of the problems facing the veterans as most members of the committee would have liked to have the privilege of doing. Of course chief of all those problems that had to be omitted from the discussion was this question of the further assistance that was necessary for the recipients of war veterans allowances. I am not going into the details of that allowance or of the requisites which are necessary in order to really place these old sailors, soldiers and airmen in a position in which they can live with dignity during their remaining years.
Some reference has been made to the change in the casual earnings earlier in this session. I know the minister will recall that I raised the question with him before Christmas, as to the exact meaning of the definition of casual earnings as given in the directive

which was then in existence. I expressed my appreciation to the minister for having looked into that question, and having produced the new directive to which the hon. member for Cape Breton South referred earlier. The casual earnings, and the expansion of the definition of casual earnings are only half the battle because the majority of the recipients of war veterans allowances are not in a position to go out and augment their allowances by undertaking work even of a casual nature. Many of those who are partially crippled, and are in receipt of a pension, of course are not in a position to augment their allowance in the least.
I merely mention that as being one of the items of unfinished business which remain today, so far as veterans affairs are concerned. And I want to offer to the minister this evening what appears to me to be a practical and timely suggestion as to the way in which these two items to which I have referred-the success of the committee and the amount of the unfinished business-can be harmonized in the future.
I would call attention to the fact that the veterans charter was drawn up and published nine years ago; it will be ten years when the next session of parliament will be called. And I would call attention to the final paragraph of the foreword written for the veterans charter by the then minister of veterans affairs, the late Hon. Ian Mackenzie, than whom no one worked harder for the veterans. This is what he wrote:
Not for ten, perhaps twenty, years will it be known how much ex-service men and women have been able to contribute to a Canada at peace as a result of these re-establishment measures. When that accounting is made, I know the program laid down in the veterans charter will appear in true perspective as a social investment of unmatched success.
And then, in the closing chapter he had these words:
The veterans charter is, therefore, not only an expression of the gratitude and generous thought of their compatriots but it is a long range plan to utilize the best minds and talents of a generation in such a way as to make an ever growing contribution to the Dominion of Canada. A contribution that in its fulfilment would enhance the social, economic and cultural advance of a nation which twice in its short history had thrust upon it a battle for survival, and under the threat of conquest had still the moral courage to plan for a nobler fulfilment of its destiny.
Those words were written ten years ago. Since the veterans charter was introduced there have been many amendments to some of the bills embraced within it. There are actually 19 different acts in the charter affecting the welfare of the veterans, and in addition there are a number of regulations.
But, as I say, this was drawn up 10 years ago; and if we allow our minds to turn

back over those ten years we will see that we have a very different world today from the atmosphere in which the charter was prepared. Ten years ago we were basking in the sunshine of the San Francisco agreement in which there were to be united nations, where five great powers were going to see that there would be no more war. That was the atmosphere in which the charter was drawn up.
We have passed from the high explosives age to the atomic age of today. But we have also made progress in many other lines. I would call attention of hon. members to the progress which has been made throughout Canada in many lines of social security, and the assistance given to those who are less fortunate than the majority. I would call attention to the assistance given under the various schemes for national health, given not only by the federal government but by many of the provinces. In those days there were no provincial health insurance plans.
Therefore I am going to suggest that next year, when parliament assembles for its next session, there should be a complete review of the veterans charter in order to bring it up to date, in order to consolidate the different acts, and in order to bring in all the different amendments so that they may be embodied in the acts. Let us see that those 19 acts are related one to the other, and also related to conditions as they exist in Canada today.
Now that the first ten years have passed we have reached the time for the first accounting, to which the late Ian Mackenzie referred. I believe we shall find that in very large measure the charter will appear in true perspective and that it will be considered an unmatched success. But we are not going to stand still. Conditions have changed in the last ten years. Now is the time for us to have that review so as to bringing the veterans charter up to date, so that it can be related to conditions as they are in Canada today, and so that a committee, set up early in the session, would have the opportunity of reviewing all those acts of parliament which have reference to the veterans of this country.

Mr. Chairman, I feel it is always wise for one to give expression to any words of commendation he may feel before proceeding to words of censure or criticism. Therefore this evening, rising to take part in this debate, I should like first of all to let the Minister of Veterans Affairs know that we appreciate deeply the readiness with which he and his department deal with all veterans problems we bring to their attention from time to time. Personally, I have always found them to be more than
Supply-Veterans Affairs ready and willing to investigate any particular case, to report upon it and to let us know the situation as it really exists.
We are also very happy in respect of those measures passed at this session of parliament. I may say that already some of the veterans in my own riding are receiving benefits from some of those measures, or they will be in the near future. Therefore first of all I commend the minister and his department.
Having done that I feel I am now free to go ahead and voice any criticisms I have with just as great emphasis as I have used in my commendation. It is not my purpose tonight to deal at length with veterans legislation in general. The hon. member for Acadia and the hon. member for New Westminster have set forth clearly our attitude with respect to veterans legislation in general. However I do feel that up to the present time the government has failed to deal with those problems that are of special concern to veterans organizations across Canada.
Speaking in the house some time ago I gave expression to that conviction, and since that time the conviction has been strengthened further by a considerable number of communications I have received from individual veterans and from branches of the Legion in various sections. I hope the saying is still true that the constant dropping of water wears away the rock-and, applying it in this instance, that the constant emphasis and re-emphasis of these particular issues will soften the heart of the government. I do not say the heart of the minister because I believe that he personally would be most happy if he could do something further for the war veterans who are not on the allowance at the present time. But I do trust that the continued re-emphasis of these particular matters will somehow encourage the government to take time off to reconsider them and give further attention to the plight of the war veterans.
The first one of course, as I have already said, is the war veterans allowance, which is recommendation No. 1 in the brief presented to the Prime Minister of Canada and the cabinet by the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League on November 10, 1953, which states:
That the basic rate of war veterans allowance be increased to $60 per month for a single veteran, and $120 per month for those who are married.
The government has already given us to understand in no uncertain terms that they are not going * to consider the raising of the war veterans allowance at this session. Some time ago this matter was brought to the

Supply-Veterans Affairs attention of the government and it was sidetracked on several occasions. Just recently I received telegrams from various Legion branches in my own particular riding. I should like to refer to a telegram that I received from W. Cross, zone commander, New Westminster and district zones of the Canadian Legion. It is dated May 21 and reads as follows:
Canadian Legion delegates from South Burnaby, New Westminster, Mission, Haney, Port Coquitlam and Port Moody branches representing 4,200 members met last night in South Burnaby branch 83 and passed unanimous motion deeply deploring Prime Minister's callousness over plight of thousands of veterans. Have wired Prime Minister. We in your constituency demand your support of Canadian Legion brief and urge you do your utmost to have War Veterans Allowance Act given full consideration this session.
I would have been as happy to see the word "request" used in the telegram instead of "demand", but the word "demand" was used. Perhaps some hon. members will recall that I brought this to the attention of the house just before the orders of the day on May 21, and asked whether the Prime Minister had received a telegram in this connection and whether he was prepared to make any statement in regard to its contents. Mr. Speaker gave me to understand that that was not the proper time to bring a question of that kind to the attention of the house, and suggested that it would be more appropriate to ask it in the veterans affairs committee or when the estimates of the Minister of Veterans Affairs were before the house. I understand that this is the proper time to refer to it. However there was no opportunity for a statement to be made at that time. I want to bring to the attention of the committee, of the minister and of the department the fact that we are still definitely interested in and concerned about this particular matter, and request that it be given full consideration, and that something further be done for those who are recipients of the war veterans allowance.
I will not refer to the veterans affairs committee. I was not a member of it, but I read some interesting things that came out of it. I was surprised at the attitude of some of the members of that committee, but I do not want to be ruled out of order at this time. Therefore I shall not make any further comments in that regard.
The second recommendation in the Canadian Legion brief to which I have referred reads:
That the ceilings on total permissible income under War Veterans Allowance Act be increased to $1,200 per year in the case of a single recipient and $2,000 per year in the case of those married.

I want to lend my support to that recommendation as well and to ask the government whether they will not just bend a little. I do not think it is asking very much, but I would request the government to bend a little and yield to the requests of the Legion in this particular respect.
I stated some time ago that I could not understand why the government refuses to raise the ceiling on permissive income. We all recognize that as it stands now it is entirely inadequate to permit of a decent standard of living. In a letter which is quoted in the October issue of the Legionary, and which was sent to the Prime Minister by C. B. Lumsden, dominion president of the Canadian Legion, we find the following in the first part of it:
For some years we have been asking for a revision of the War Veterans Allowance Act which would raise the ceiling on permissible income and permit an increase in the basic allowance for those with no other means of support. To us the moral and sociological reasons in favour of these changes seem overwhelming and our members find it difficult to understand why our representations have not been accepted.
There is little that we can add to the briefs previously presented. We would merely like to reiterate that as the act stands at present it tends to defeat its own objectives. If the allowance is intended to assist the aged and needy veteran, the low permissive ceiling prevents him from supplementing this allowance sufficiently to enjoy a reasonable standard of living. If it is intended as a subsistence allowance, it is far too small.
The taxation laws of Canada consider that an income of less than $2,000 is too low for a married man to pay income tax. Yet war veterans allowance expects a married couple to live on $1,200 a year.
There is more to the letter but I will not take the time of the committee to read it. I should like to suggest once again that the government give consideration and take action as soon as possible to accede to the request of the Legion. These are the two matters to which I should like to refer. I know other speakers have already emphasized them, but I want to give them my support at this time. I urge the government to yield on these two important and very necessary requests.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I believe
that there are 243 members of this house who not only would offer no objection but who would welcome it wholeheartedly if tomorrow morning at eleven o'clock the Prime Minister were to announce on behalf of the government its desire to bring in an amendment to the War Veterans Allowance Act, and were to ask the house for unanimous consent to put it through all stages at one sitting. The legislation would be passed before one o'clock tomorrow.

I use the figure of 243 members advisedly. There are 265 seats in this house. We are missing two whom we lost a short while ago. There are 20 members of this house who are in the cabinet. That leaves 243 of us who are private members. I suggest that all 243 of us would readily agree to such a request if the government were to make it tomorrow morning. I urge that consideration be given to that proposition.
It has been suggested by a good many members during the course of the debate today that something must be done about this matter as soon as possible, and certainly at the next session of parliament. I see no reason why it should not be done at this session even yet, certainly before we reach prorogation.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, this debate is a demonstration of the way in which parliament sometimes works. As I have already said, we are 265 members when we are all here, but for those of us outside of the cabinet all we can do is make speeches, move amendments, ask questions, and do all the other things we can to try to persuade the government to bring in legislation of this kind.
When it comes to legislation of almost any kind, and particularly when it comes to legislation involving the expenditure of money, that must be brought in by the government. Those 20 men in the cabinet-and I am referring to the 20 who are members of this house because although there are 21 members in the cabinet one of them is over in the other place- occupy a key position. What it boils down to is this, that 11 of those 20 occupy the key position. Eleven out of those 20 would constitute a majority. What the other 243 members of this house are doing is making appeals of this kind in the hope that we can yet persuade 11 out of those 20 to agree that something should be done about this matter at this session of parliament.
Let it not be said that it is too late. As a matter of fact, during this very week a piece of legislation is being put through, notice of which was not given until Monday. I realize that it turns out to be an uncontentious piece of legislation. I refer to the proposal to amend the Judges Act-but not to increase the salaries of judges-and I would point out that notice of that intention was not given until Monday of this week. Unanimous consent has not yet been requested for the purpose of speeding up the progress of that legislation. If it goes through its normal stages at the speed permitted by the rule book it could be through by Friday of this week. In other sessions there have been instances where items of legislation have been brought in near the end of the session and have been
Supply-Veterans Affairs put through all their necessary stages. That could certainly be done with this piece of legislation and I urge that even yet consideration be given to it. I do not know of any reason why a cabinet meeting could not be held tonight or tomorrow morning in time for the opening of this house at eleven o'clock. If the cabinet cannot meet before tomorrow morning, we are meeting Saturday and that would be a good way in which to start Saturday sittings in this session, namely, by having amendments brought in to the War Veterans Allowance Act.
Now, Mr. Chairman, reference has been made quite frequently this evening to the report of the veterans affairs committee. I do not think the recommendation to which reference has been made has yet been put on the record in its entirety and I think we should have that part of the report before us in its exact terms. Before reading it I would like to point out that this is from the fifth report of the special committee on veterans affairs which was presented to the house by the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Rosthern, on Friday, June 11. The part to which reference has been so frequently made reads as follows:
In tabling herewith a copy of the evidence adduced, your committee desires to draw attention to the fact that the submission by the Canadian Legion, the National Council of Veterans Associations and the Canadian non-pensioned veterans' widows, each contained, in addition to representations in respect of the said bills,-
That refers to the four bills which were before the committee.
-representations urging changes in the War Veterans Allowance Act to raise the amounts of allowances payable thereunder, and also to raise the level of permissive income.
The Canadian Merchant Navy Veterans Association, in their submission, laid most stress on a wish that those who served during world war II in dangerous waters receive the benefits of the Veterans Land Act.
Your committee recommends that the government give sympathetic consideration to the said submissions.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I must say that I rather share the views of those who have characterized that last sentence as something in the nature of a pious hope or a pious prayer, but at least we do know that after all the arguments were over in the committee that report was adopted unanimously.
Now, who made up that committee? It was made up of private members chosen from amongst the 243 to whom I referred a few minutes ago, representing all the parties in this house. I submit that the fact that those members representing the various parties in this house agreed unanimously on this report makes it crystal clear that not only those members in the committee but the
6190	HOUSE OF
Supply-Veterans Affairs entire 243 support that contention that the government should give sympathetic consideration to these submissions. The first of these submissions was that the War Veterans Allowance Act should be amended to raise the amount of the allowance payable thereunder, and also to raise the level of permissive income.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I could but I do not think it is necessary to go into the merits of the case itself. The reason why it is not necessary is because it is so obvious, and because it has been made so many times this afternoon and evening. But I feel I would like to pinpoint the fact that here is an opportunity for the government to recognize the way in which parliament properly works. Here is an opportunity for the government to recognize the wish of the 243 of us who are here, and respond to the unanimous feeling of the private members of this house.
I know there has been no vote in which the 243 members have had a chance to express themselves, but I think I am perfectly justified in contending that the unanimous support of this report by members representing all parties means that the 243 of us would welcome action on this matter at this session, and I hope that even yet, before we reach the day of prorogation, something will be done about this matter.
For my part I support the contention that has been made by the Canadian Legion that the amount of the allowance should be increased to not less than $60 a month single and $120 a month married. I agree too with the contention of the Legion that if it is not possible to remove the means test altogether then at least the level of permissive income should be raised to $1,200 a year single, and $2,000 a year married.
I think particular notice should be taken of the fact that amongst those who appeared before the committee were representatives of the Canadian non-pensioned veterans widows association. As hon. members know there was a time when there was no provision for non-pensioned veterans widows and then the time came along about 1943 when, by an item in the estimates, there was a special allowance for these women. In due course their allowance was made statutory by their being brought under the terms of the War Veterans Allowance Act. Therefore when we are asking for these increases under the War Veterans Allowance Act we are quite properly asking for an increase, not only for the war veterans themselves who are the recipients of those allowances but for the widows who qualify under this same legislation, and I wish to support their other requests as well.
fMr. Knowles.]

I wish to indicate once again my support of the contention which has been made repeatedly, and made many times today, that something should be done about that cut-off date with respect to the widows of imperial veterans. It seems to me that some change in that provision should be made so that it will not be necessary for the veteran to have lived in Canada the full 20 years in order for his widow to qualify. This provision results in many cases of hardship, which could be avoided by changing that 20 year provision.
I support the contention made earlier today that surely the time has come when the United Kingdom might be recognized as a theatre of war so far as world war I is concerned. This has been a sore point for a long time. The number affected by it is dwindling all the time. It has become more of an issue now that the United Kingdom has been accepted as a theatre of war in world war II. I submit that to make this change would have value not only in terms of the dollars that would be available to many of these veterans or to some of their widows as the result of the change but as a boost in morale to our older veterans generally. I hope that even yet that change might be made.
As I have already indicated, Mr. Chairman, the case for amending the War Veterans Allowance Act in terms of substance, in terms of the merits of the matter and in terms of what our veterans deserve has been made so well at this session and at other sessions across the years that it is hardly necessary to repeat it. I urge as strongly as I can, and as seriously and as earnestly as I can, that this matter be not left over as an item of unfinished business for another session but that something be done about it at this session. I see no reason why the Prime Minister should not announce the desire and willingness of the government to bring in such a bill tomorrow morning at eleven o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, it has been significant that throughout the debate this afternoon and this evening, practically all of the attention has been focused on the war veterans allowance. I think I have never before seen a debate on veterans affairs proceed in that way. There is, of course, a reason for this fact. The plight of the war veterans allowance recipients and of those who might qualify if the restrictions were not so severe is the most serious situation facing the veterans of Canada today.
These men must have been fighting men. No one can qualify for the war veterans allowance unless he served in a theatre of

war, with the exception of those who are in receipt of a pension for a disability or an injury suffered in England or in Canada during the first war; and of course there is a similar eligibility for the veterans of the second world war.
And those with dual service.

Yes; there are also the men who had dual service. These men have a good claim to consideration by the government because, as I have said, they have been our fighting men. Not only have they a good claim but there is great importance to this question because time is so vital. They are now reaching an age when many of them are dropping off. Within the next year probably many hundreds of these men will die. They are facing not a deadline such as that which has been written into the Pension Act, but a death-line. Hence time is of the utmost importance.
There is one thing that stands out clearly today and it is that there will be no action whatever to help these veterans at the present session. Next year something may be done for them, but it is absolutely clear that nothing is to be done at this session. That fact, I submit, is the tragedy of this whole situation.
The primary responsibility for failure to act at this session rests squarely on the government. Recommendations were made to them unanimously two years ago by a special committee on veterans affairs set up in the session of that year. I have here a copy of the report which was dated June 18, 1952, and contains this recommendation with regard to war veterans allowance:
Your committee further recommends to the government continued and sympathetic study of the needs and requirements of recipients of war veterans' allowance, keeping in mind the recommendations of veterans' organizations in that respect and particularly with regard to permissive income.
Some of us on that committee had tried to get through a resolution which called for action at the session of 1952, but the best we could do was this recommendation which I have read. It was made unanimously. Every member on that committee supported that recommendation. However no action has been taken by the government during the intervening two years, with the exception of some modification in the definition of what constitutes casual earnings.
Then recommendations on this question were made by the Canadian Legion every year. On November 10 of last year they submitted to the cabinet a brief which contained their recommendations, once again, for improvement of the War Veterans Allowance Act. They asked that the maximum payment
Supply-Veterans Affairs to the single veteran be increased from $50 a month to $60, that the maximum payment to the married veteran be increased from $90 to $120, and that the ceiling on permissive income should be $1,200 for the single veteran and $2,000 for the married veteran.
Then we had put on the order paper, early in the spring, the motion for the setting up of a committee on veterans affairs. The government chose to word that motion in such a way that the committee had power to deal only with what bills were referred to it; and the Prime Minister announced that there would not be any amendment to the War Veterans Allowance Act at this session. There was therefore no prospect of having the War Veterans Allowance Act referred to the committee.
During the debate in the house on the setting up of the committee we sought to have the terms of reference widened in order to enable the committee to deal with the war veterans allowance, but the government refused to accept that suggestion. I had thought that as a result of the debate in the house the government might change its attitude.
I think perhaps that change of attitude might have taken place if private members on the government side of the house had taken a determined stand asking that the terms of reference be extended. However, only one or two of them did so. Mind you, Mr. Chairman, I realize that it is a great deal more difficult for a supporter of the government to rise in his place and criticize the government than it is for those of us who are on the opposition side to do so. However, in this instance I feel confident that if the Liberal members had been a little bit tougher at the time of the setting up of that committee we might not today be placed in the unfortunate position that nothing is to be done at the present session in the way of improving the war veterans allowance. I therefore repeat that the primary responsibility rests squarely on the government.
I do not blame the veterans affairs committee to the same extent, but I say that our committee on veterans affairs lost a splendid opportunity to bring about improvements. We heard representations from the Legion although the terms of reference were not supposed to include consideration of the war veterans allowance. We also had a brief from the national council in which they regretted that the war veterans allowance could not be considered at this session. When we came to consider what action should be taken by the committee some of us tried to put through a motion which would have had

Supply-Veterans Affairs the effect of asking the house to widen the terms of reference. That motion read as follows:
That this committee submit a report to the house requesting that the terms of reference of the committee be enlarged to enable it to consider the War Veterans Allowance Act and make recommendations in respect thereof at this session of parliament.
That motion was ruled out of order by the chairman of the committee. He needed a good many law books and rule books and a very long argument in order to arrive finally at the decision that the motion was out of order. However, he did so rule. But I point out, Mr. Chairman, that every committee is master of its own fate. The members of that committee had the power to overrule the ruling which had been made by the chairman, and an appeal was taken to the committee as a whole against that ruling. We voted on that appeal. The government members lined up solidly behind the chairman. There again I can see a reason for their doing so. I regretted that they did, but it was much easier for those of us in the opposition to vote against the chairman's ruling than it was for the supporters of the government.
But quite frankly I find it very hard to understand why the hon. member for Cape Breton South and the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary saw fit to vote in support of the chairman's ruling because if it had been upset there is no doubt that the motion itself would have carried and we would have come back to the house with a recommendation that the terms of reference of the committee be extended so that it could consider the question of the war veterans allowance. However, they voted that way. Their colleague, the hon. member for Kootenay West, voted the other way. He justified his position in the committee and has done so in the house today.
In the final analysis a report was brought in by the committee to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has referred, and it does contain this reference:
Your committee recommends that the government give sympathetic consideration to the said submissions.
That included the submissions on the question of the war veterans allowance. I believe that the report should have gone further and that it should have recommended that legislation amending the War Veterans Allowance Act be introduced at the present session of parliament. However, we do have this report recommending consideration. It has the value of placing before the government again the need for considering the question of the war veterans allowance, but it has the terrible

weakness that no possible action can be taken at the present session to help recipients of the allowance. That, I think, is one of the saddest situations in which I have seen the veterans of this country placed since I came here in 1935.
This is a dangerous situation for the veterans of Canada for another reason. I believe that the government is refusing to do anything about the war veterans allowance because it is government policy to treat the war veterans allowance recipient on the same basis as ordinary civilian welfare cases. I believe that is the secret of the refusal of the government to listen to these various recommendations. Just a few days ago a bill was passed in the house known as the Disabled Persons Act. It is significant to note that the maximum amount that a disabled person who qualifies under the act can get is $720 a year if he or she is single and $1,200 a year if married. There you have the same ceilings that exist in the War Veterans Allowance Act.
Then we go back to 1951 to the Old Age Assistance Act. There again there is a ceiling of $720 for the single recipient and $1,200 for the married. Thus it becomes perfectly clear that the plan is to keep these old frontline soldiers on the same basis as civilians who are getting benefits under these civilian acts. As hon. members have pointed out, one result of that is that in British Columbia and Alberta today the civilian is getting more than the war veterans allowance recipient.
But the fundamental mistake in the government's policy is that the claim of the war veterans allowance man is completely different from that of the civilian. The civilian gets these payments as a matter of welfare. The war veterans allowance man gets them because he risked his life for his country. His claim is for services rendered and he should not be put on the same basis as the civilian. He has a claim as of right. I believe that every member of the house down in his heart knows that such is the case and that there is that great distinction between these two groups. I believe it is a tragedy that the government is failing to recognize that difference and is forcing these war veterans allowance men to remain in the same position as welfare recipients.
That is not what the members of the house wish, no matter to what party they belong. It is not what the newspapers of this country wish. I daresay there have been editorials in every leading paper in Canada in favour of doing something for these fighting troops. It is not what the Canadian people wish, whether they be young or old, whether they be old comrades of these war veterans allowance men or whether they be civilians. They

want to see these fighting men treated in a fair way and treated on the basis of having earned the right to receive this help from their country. I do not believe there is a person in Canada who would be unwilling to see money put out to increase the war veterans allowance to the amount set by the Legion and to raise the ceiling on permissive income to the amounts the Legion requests.
There you have the reason why this is a fighting issue. This issue is not going to be allowed to drop by members of the house who have taken their stand for years, or by the newspapers of the country or by the veterans organizations. I hope that the Canadian people will insist that the just claims of these veterans be recognized. I can only add in closing that I think it is a terrible tragedy that nothing is to be done for these fighting men at the present session.

I should like at the start, Mr. Chairman, to heartily endorse the suggestion made by my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, because I am quite sure he was right when he expressed the view there is not a single one of the 243 private members of the house who would oppose this measure. In fact, I would think this would be an opportunity for some of them to get up and say if they do oppose that suggestion. I do not see any of them getting up, so I presume we can take it for granted that they all agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Speak now or forever hold your peace.

I am at a loss to understand why this government periodically persists in doing something so stupid as they have done with regard to the war veterans allowances. There can only be one of two reasons that makes them decline the demands of not only the veterans organizations but of the citizens of Canada. I am quite sure there is not a member in this house who does not feel a sense of shame when he reads in the newspaper the sort of case referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver South. There can be no member in this house who tonight does not feel a sense of shame when he knows that if the government persists in its foolish, stupid opposition, before the house meets again there are going to be many more old men and old women who are going to turn on the gas. We all know that. They are going to turn it on and stick their heads in the oven. I would not consider it advisable for any member to treat this matter with levity, because it is not such a matter. It is a matter for shame for all decent Canadian citizens.
Supply-Veterans Affairs
As I say, there is only one of two reasons. One is that they consider the veterans of two world wars do not deserve any greater measure of generosity than parliament has already granted them. I doubt if there is any member of this house who would have the foolhardiness to rise and suggest that that is a reasonable cause for the government's position. I doubt if there is anyone here who would have the temerity to get up and say that the man who risked his life for Canada is not worth more than he is getting now under the legislation. There may be some, but I doubt if there are any in this chamber who would dare get up and say so.
I am not suggesting that all those who joined the armed forces and fought in Canada's wars were heroes. We were not heroes. They are few and far between. It is time, however, I believe for this government to be reminded of the fact that every man who joins the armed forces of this country takes the risk that he is going to lose his life in that service. He takes another risk, too, in fact it is almost a certainty. He runs an almost certain risk of damaging himself physically or psychologically or both. It has been stated that most of the veterans of the first world war can be considered medically some ten years older than their calendar age. I do not know whether or not that is true, but I have heard that reported on many occasions. I am quite sure a very large majority of those who went through the four years of the first war came back to Canada impaired in some way in their health. I doubt whether that is the reason the government is declining to do this.
The only other reason is that we cannot afford it. I do not know what it would cost to implement the demands of the Canadian Legion. I do not know whether it would mean adding 50 per cent or 100 per cent to the present expenditure of $27 million on war veterans allowances. But even if it cost 100 per cent more, even if it means our bill for war veterans allowance will be doubled, and we will have to spend another $27 million, I think that is a very weak and shaky reason for refusing to do it. This $27 million is a lot of money, and of course the government may perhaps hesitate to ask the taxpayers of Canada to dig into their pockets to find another $27 million.
On the other hand the government apparently had not the slightest hesitation or compunction in not asking but forcing the taxpayers of Canada to dig into their pockets to the tune of $277 million, since the Department of Defence Production was established, as an allowance for write-offs on income tax

Supply-Veterans Affairs for those firms that are patriotically providing the sinews of war. The amount is reported here as $277 million that has been accorded these people by way of additional benefits in income tax write-offs since the Department of Defence Production was established in 1951. The government had no hesitation whatever in digging into the pockets of the Canadian taxpayer to the tune of $48 million in order to make grants of additional working capital for one year, 1953, to those firms that are producing the sinews of war which may be used by future generations of Canadian veterans who will have to get along on $40 per month.
I am going to suggest that the government had better tell the people of Canada very bluntly and plainly just why they consider that the gentlemen who own the industries, many of these industries which were apparently built by public funds and which provide the sinews of war, are more worthy of aid from the public treasury than are the men who came back from two wars. I wonder, Mr. Chairman, how much we are paying in the way of profits on the expenditures we are going to make this year of $160 million on naval equipment; $80 million on army equipment and nearly $447 million on air force equipment, a total of some $688 million on military equipment for which orders are being placed this year according to the estimates before us. I wonder what percentage of that is going in perhaps not exactly justifiable profits to those who own those industries. I wonder whether perhaps we might consider that one per cent or two per cent of that volume might be exceptional profits, profits to which one could reasonably take exception.
If they were, of course, and if we decided not to give it to those operating these industries we would have ample funds to implement the Legion's demands. This would allow some sort of justice to be accorded to the old men, who once were young and who in the days of their youth gave their services to the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
In, rising to speak on this item of the departmental estimates, Mr. Chairman, I feel that at the very beginning I should offer my thanks and those of the government to the members of the veterans affairs committee who this year have made a thorough study in their usual efficient manner of the legislation referred to them by this house. I recognize that on this committee there are some veterans, not of wars but of the committee's work, and there are also some new members who made a fine contribution.
I would like to thank at the same time the various veterans organizations, the Canadian

Legion, the National Council of Veterans Associations, the non-pensioned widows and the merchant seamen who came before the committee, presented briefs and made representations in their usual constructive manner.
Since the debate began this afternoon many subjects have been discussed by hon. members who have participated. I believe some of these matters could be answered more appropriately when we are discussing the specific items in the estimates dealing with the matters concerned. However it is obvious that the whole debate has centred on this very serious question of war veterans allowances. Observations have been made which I believe call for some rectification on my part, or at least for a statement of certain facts which may have been overlooked in discussing the matter.
I am not saying for one moment that the matter has not been discussed properly by hon. members. However I do feel that certain terms used in the house and outside of it with reference to war veterans allowances have been somewhat exaggerated, and that the use of words such as indifferent, callousness and stupidity as regards this administration is indicative of a lack of comprehension of all the implications of this particular question.
I do not want to go over the whole history of war veterans allowances. However I do believe that in order to understand exactly the position of the government in considering this question the picture should be made clear. I say this because to many of us who are familiar with veterans legislation, such as members of the committee who have been sitting for some years and following that legislation, it appears very clear; to some members of the press who have followed it it is also clear. However, at least to myself and others who are receiving representations from outside, and who are reading certain editorials in the press, it is plain there is uncertainty in the public mind as to what war veterans allowances are. In many people's minds there appears to be confusion between war veterans allowances and disability pensions.
I say this because I have received many letters in which it is pointed out that something should be done about raising the war veterans allowance for the old wounded veterans. In other words, in the minds of many people there is no appreciation of the fact that war veterans allowances and pensions for disability incurred during service are/ two different things.	/
The war veterans allowance was instituted in 1930. I thought the hon. member for Acadia stated the situation very clearly this

afternoon. It was created for the purpose of looking after the older veterans, and making available to them the old age pension, as it was called at that time, ten years before any other citizens were eligible to receive it, on the basis that active service in the front line would cause pre-ageing by ten years in any man who had been called upon to perform in the front line. Consequently those who could qualify under the original act were veterans who were sixty years of age, and those who, being under sixty years, could be certified to be totally disabled and incapacitated. No others qualified. The benefit given at that time was that they could receive the equivalent of the old age pension, under the same conditions of a means test and, as I have said, ten years sooner.
What has happened since then? Well, of course the act has been widened, and new groups have been admitted. Widows and dual service veterans have been brought in. Veterans have also been made eligible whose circumstances were such that as a result of the combination of their financial circumstances and their physical condition they have found it impossible to find work in the labour market.
Furthermore, all through the history of this legislation the amount paid by way of war veterans allowances, and the ceilings imposed under the means test, were always parallel to those of the old age pension, for the reason given this afternoon by the hon. member for Acadia-that at the very beginning it was stated that the purpose of the legislation was to make old age pensions available to older veterans ten years before other citizens in this country were so eligible.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra says he knows the secret as to why the government will not accede to the demands being made. He said it is because we are assimilating these veterans into the civilian population, and giving them the same treatment as civilians. There is no secret about this. That has been said right along, ever since the act was created. I repeated it last year and I said that I could not see how a major change could be made in this legislation which would break the ties that have existed between war veterans allowances and old age pensions, a relationship which has always existed between those two pieces of legislation.
Remove the means test.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I shall deal with this matter.
What is the situation at the present time? I should like to give a few figures in order to show that in spite of what has been said here tonight the government has considered this
Supply-Veterans Affairs question very seriously, that there are important factors to be considered before making any changes in the legislation, and that the implications may well be more far-reaching than is understood by at least some hon. members opposite.
At the present time the estimates indicate that the item for the war veterans allowance, together with the assistance fund, total $27,715,500. This amount has been increasing in the last ten years. I believe that ten years ago it was about $14 million. However this increase is a normal process. Another factor which must be considered in the cost of war veterans allowances is that the recipients of the allowance are also entitled to free medical treatment. And, although the money expended for medical treatment for the recipients of the war veterans allowance does not appear in a separate item in the estimates, the cost in the last fiscal year was $8,992,850, or just a few thousand dollars less than $9 million. This sum should be added to the $27 million I have just mentioned.
What would happen from the point of view of increasing liability if at the present time increases, as some have been suggesting, were adopted by the government?
It has been suggested that the allowance should be increased from $50 to $60 for a single recipient and from $90 to $120 for the married recipient, and at the same time the ceilings should be raised to $1,200 for the single recipient and to $2,000 for the married recipient. That alone, sir, would increase the present liability for war veterans allowance by over $16 million. That is, it would increase the expenditure for the present year by 60 per cent, on the basis of the present number of recipients; but to that must be added an estimated $2,500,000 for additional recipients, which must necessarily follow from the fact that the ceiling is raised. As hon. members know, every time the ceiling is raised in legislation such as this new groups of people qualify and the expenditure is thereby increased. Therefore, at the present time, to give the increases both in the amount and in the ceilings that I have mentioned would raise our present liability for war veterans allowances to an amount between $46 million and $47 million. This is far from the $3 million that has been mentioned by certain members. And I can assure this committee that these estimates are very conservative indeed.

May I ask the minister a question? Can he break that down into the amount that it would cost to increase the ceiling on permissive income?

Supply-Veterans Affairs

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I am sorry, I have not the figure which would show the increase in cost simply by increasing the ceiling to $1,200 and $2,000; but I have had computations made, and to raise the ceiling from $720 to only $840 for the single person and from $1,200 to $1,440 for the married person would cost approximately $4 million, and that is of course without increasing the amount of payment to the present number of recipients.
It has also been represented that besides the increases which we are asked to grant, the benefits of the act should be made available to veterans who served in the United Kingdom only during the first war, in the same way as those who served in the United Kingdom during the second war receive them. Well, there again, Mr. Chairman, that item alone is estimated to increase the annual liability by $5,670,000.
Therefore, the points that I have mentioned, namely, increasing the amounts, increasing the ceilings and making the allowance available to world war I veterans who served in the United Kingdom only, would increase the annual liability at this time from $27,750,000 to over $52 million, or an increase of approximately 95 per cent. Whether that should be done or not is certainly a matter to be decided only after serious consideration. I am simply putting these facts and figures before the committee so that it will be realized that before taking a major decision such as this the government has some very important factors to consider.
There are other aspects of the question which I believe the government and the committee must consider also, and they should be put on the record. There is the effect that the increase in ceilings would have, and I am speaking of course of the suggestion to increase the ceilings to $1,200 for the single recipient and to $2,000 for the married recipient. At the present time a single man receiving war veterans allowance, if he can supplement his allowance, can receive up to $720, which represents a disability pension of about 50 per cent, the full pension being $1,500. A married man, if he supplements his allowance, can receive the equivalent of what a married 60 per cent disability pensioner receives.
I should like to point out that ever since this act was put on the statute books of Canada there has always been a correlation between the war veterans allowance and the Pension Act; that is, the amounts paid under the War Veterans Allowance Act have always borne a relationship to what could be paid under the Pension Act. If the present ceilings were raised, it would mean that a single veteran could get the equivalent of a 75

per cent disability pension, although he might not be pensioned at all, and the married veteran could get up to the equivalent of a 95 per cent disability pension. A 100 per cent disability pension, as hon. members know, is $2,040.
May I ask the minister this question? If the rate for a single recipient of war veterans allowance is raised to $60 that certainly is not 75 per cent. Did the minister say that?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I am sorry; I did not make myself clear. I was speaking of the proposed ceiling of $2,000 for the married recipient.
The government does not pay that.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: No.
That is what he is able to earn.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: That is correct. In other words, the 30 per cent disability pensioner who is single could supplement his disability pension and receive the same amount as a 75 per cent disability pensioner, the amount coming both from the pension commission and the war veterans allowance board. The married 25 per cent disability pensioner could supplement his disability pension through war veterans allowances so that it would be the equivalent of a 95 per cent disability pension. I am simply pointing that out because it is certainly not the usual relation that has existed between the payments made under the two acts. Whether this is desirable or not and whether the seriously disabled veterans of this country and the public would like such a state of affairs to exist is something which the government must necessarily take into consideration.
But all the veterans are asking for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I have heard many representations. There is another aspect which must be considered and which may be of some interest to the committee; for instance if the ceiling of $2,000 was put into the act many veterans in steady employment, including some who are permanent lower grade employees in the civil service, would be supplementing the regular salary which they are earning with the war veterans allowance. I know that in the Department of Veterans Affairs there are very many classifications of employees in the lower grades who are receiving salaries under $2,000. These employees, if married, would be supplementing their salary. It may be said that they should be receiving more, but I would suggest

that the War Veterans Allowance Act was not conceived to be an instrument through which such adjustments should be made.
Not only that, but a great number of retired civil servants who have 20, 25 or more years' service in positions paying $3,000, $3,500, and up to $4,000 would be able through war veterans allowance to supplement their superannuation of less than $2,000 to which they are entitled under the Public Service Superannuation Act.
As a matter of fact in my own department I have found that in the last year there have been 66 employees with salaries of $3,000 or under, who were retired after having completed an average of 22 years service in the department. Now, under the Public Service Superannuation Act their retirement pension will average $805 per year. Each one of those who was a veteran who had served overseas would qualify under the provisions of the act, thus enabling him to supplement his superannuation to the amount of $2,000, which, in many cases, would be the equivalent of the salary at which he retired.
I am simply putting these facts before the house in order to emphasize that this matter has been under consideration, that the government has given the subject a thorough study, and in fact is still doing so. I can assure hon. members that the recommendations made by the veterans affairs committee to the effect that this matter should be considered with sympathy by the government will receive the attention of my colleagues and myself. In fact, this legislation, as well as all other veterans' legislation, is continually under survey within my own department. I give it all the consideration possible within my own limited capacity, and it is also given consideration by my colleagues. That is evidenced by some of the facts which have been mentioned here today.
The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich and the hon. member for Cape Breton South made reference to the new instructions which have been issued defining casual earnings for the purpose of the War Veterans Allowance Act and I suggest that anyone who reads these instructions will agree that this is not a definition which shows any lack of generosity, or indicates callousness on the part of the government. It is a very generous definition and one which will benefit a great number of recipients. The same is the case with regard to instructions on farm income.
Would the minister put the definition regarding casual earnings on the record?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I would be very glad to do so but it is a rather extensive statement.
Supply-Veterans Affairs Mr. Quelch: There is no necessity to read it.
The minister can have unanimous consent to put it on the record.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Has the minister unanimous consent to place this definition on Hansard?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
The definition is as follows:
Re: Casual earnings
The board has made a study of all cases which have been submitted by the district authorities in accordance with W.V.A.B. directive No. 17-1953 as amended and the chairman s letter dated August 24, 1953. As a result of this study the following instructions, which will supersede previous directives on the subject, are issued to cover all types of cases and the district authorities can now deal with them on the basis of the formula outlined hereunder.
Casual earnings exempted as income by Sec. 6. (d) of the War Veterans Allowance Act in respect of recipients under Sec. 3. of that act fall into four principal categories.
(a)	Earnings by a recipient and/or his wife for work of an irregular nature commonly termed "odd jobs", i.e. small jobs complete in themselves for one or more employers.
These earnings are fully exempt.
(b)	Earnings	by	a	recipient and/or his	wife
resulting from part-time regular employment such as a caretaker for a church or school, a canteen attendant, a crossing guard, self-employment at home on a part-time basis, etc.
Earnings under this category may be exempt in an amount which will not exceed an average of two dollars per diem for 25 working days in any month.
(c)	Earnings	by	a	recipient and/or his	wife
resulting from full-time temporary employment of limited duration such as at summer camps, guard duties, collecting tickets at race tracks, replacing a regular employee on holidays, harvesting or other similar activities of relatively short duration.
Earnings under this category may be exempt for a	period or periods of employment which do not
exceed a total	of	12	weeks in any V.A.	year.
Where such period or periods exceed 12 weeks in the V.A. year only the amounts earned during the first 12 weeks may be exempt and the other earnings will be considered as income.
The district authorities will suspend payment of the War Veterans Allowance as soon as full-time employment is reported by a recipient and will make the necessary adjustments in accordance with the above principles when such employment is terminated.
(d)	A remuneration earned as a result of some isolated deal such as receiving a commission for helping sell or buy a property of or for a friend, provided such transaction is unusual, personal and direct between the recipient and the person concerned and not performed as an agent or sub-agent of a real estate firm or dealer.
Earnings under this category are fully exempt.
There may be some exceptional cases which the present directive does not appear to cover. If so, district authorities should refer such cases, with full particulars, for decision by the war veterans allowance board.
Cases which have been decided in accordance with former directives and which, if dealt with under the present directive, could be changed, may be reviewed, providing no adjustment shall be made for deductions on account of earnings prior to September 1, 1953.

As regards farm income which I understand was often a source of difficulty, we have a new definition which I think meets the demands made by the various veterans' organizations. Perquisites are no longer taken into consideration in computing the income of the farmer. Under the new formula 25 per cent on the first $1,000 gross income of the farmer veteran is considered as income, 40 per cent on the next $1,000 gross income, and 50 per cent on the third $1,000 gross income is considered as income under the act. If he prefers, he can keep an accounting of his farm operations and his net income would be established by his own books. Our own field man operating under the Veterans Land Act would help the veteran in this particular work.
I am simply mentioning these facts to show that the government always has under consideration the interests of the recipients of the war veterans allowance. Decisions in this regard are most important and have many serious implications. For the reasons I have mentioned, the government has not found it possible at this time to recommend the increases which have been requested.

Will the minister deal with this one point? On the basis of the presumption that a veteran has pre-aged by ten years, and in view of the fact that at the age of 70 the means test has been lifted for the civilian, why has not the means test been lifted at the age of 60 for the veteran?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: For one thing, I think the government would have to consider that most veterans are still working at age 60. Furthermore, I must point out to my hon. friend that this would mean that every veteran who, at one time or another, had spent one day overseas would automatically get war veterans allowance upon reaching the age of 60, whatever might be his financial circumstances. To me it is the equivalent of what is usually known as a service pension. In the past there have been discussions as to the desirability of having service pensions; that is, that every man who, at one time or another during his life, was in the active forces of Canada, by the fact of his service, whether he needed it or not or whether he was disabled or not, should receive a pension. When these discussions took place I believe the veterans organizations themselves did not press that point. They thought it was better to ask for appropriate disability pensions and various other means of assistance.
